    16	\label{sec:linear-spaces}
    17	
    18	Linear spaces are always of the form $V = \F^n$ for a finite field $\F$ and an
    19	integer $n \ge 1$, unless explicitly stated otherwise. We write $\hat{E} =
    20	\{\hat{e}_1, \dots, \hat{e}_n\}$ for the standard basis of $V$, where
    21	$\hat{e}_i$ has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere, and
    22	$\mathrm{End}(V)$ for the set of linear maps from $V$ to itself.
    23	
    24	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]\label{def:register-subspace}
    25		A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
    26		subset of the standard basis of $V$. Such a subspace is represented by an
    27		indicator vector $u \in \{0,1\}^s$, where $s = \dim(V)$, via
    28		$S = \mathrm{span}\{\hat{e}_i : u_i = 1\}$.
    29	\end{definition}
    30	
    31	\begin{definition}[Dot product and orthogonal subspace]\label{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    32		For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$ and
    33		$v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V = \F^n$, the \emph{dot product} is
    34		\[
    35			u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
    36		\]
    37		For a subspace $S$ of $V$, the \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
    38		\[
    39			S^\perp = \bigl\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0 \text{ for all } v \in S \bigr\}\;.
    40		\]
    41		The notation $S^\perp$ leaves the ambient space $V$ implicit.
    42	\end{definition}
    43	
    44	Over finite fields, orthogonality lacks some of the familiar properties it has
    45	over $\R$ or $\C$; for example, a nonzero subspace may be orthogonal to itself,
    46	as is $\mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ over $\F_2$. The following dimension identity
    47	nevertheless holds over every field.
    48	
    49	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:perp_perp}
    50		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    51		Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) = \dim(V)$, and
    52		\[
    53			(S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
    54		\]
    55	\end{lemma}
    56	\begin{proof}
    57		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    58		The elements of $S^\perp$ are the solutions of a feasible linear system whose
    59		coefficient matrix has $\dim(S)$ linearly independent rows, so the solution
    60		space has dimension exactly $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$. Every $u \in S$ is
    61		orthogonal to every element of $S^\perp$, so $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
    62		Applying the dimension identity twice shows that
    63		$\dim\bigl((S^\perp)^\perp\bigr) = \dim(S)$, so the inclusion is an equality.
    64	\end{proof}
    65	
    66	\begin{definition}[Complementary subspaces]\label{def:complementary}
    67		Two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of a linear space $V$ form a pair of
    68		\emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
    69		\[
    70			S \cap T = \{0\}\;, \qquad S + T = V\;.
    71		\]
    72		In this case we write $V = S \oplus T$. Every $x \in V$ can be written
    73		uniquely as $x = x^S + x^T$ with $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$; we call $x^S$
    74		(resp.\ $x^T$) the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel to $T$} (resp.\
    75		onto $T$ parallel to $S$). The unique linear map $L : V \to V$ with
    76		$x \mapsto x^S$ is the \emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
    77	\end{definition}
    78	
    79	A subspace may have many complementary subspaces: in $\F_2^2$, the subspace
    80	$S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ has the distinct complements
    81	$\mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and $\mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$. Given a basis of $S$,
    82	one may nevertheless single out a \emph{canonical} complement.
    83	
    84	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
    85		\uses{def:register-subspace}
    86		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
    87		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
    88		vectors. Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\, \hat{e}_j$, and, using a
    89		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
    90		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $(a_{i,j})$ to reduced row echelon form
    91		$(b_{i,j})$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
    92		$1$ entry of each row of $(b_{i,j})$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
    93		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
    94		\[
    95			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_j : j \notin J\}\;.
    96		\]
    97		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace.
    98		% Basis-independence made explicit here: the source defines F^perp through
    99		% a basis but does not assert dependence on it; uniqueness of the reduced
   100		% row echelon form gives dependence on span(F) alone.
   101		Although defined through the basis $F$, it depends only on
   102		$\mathrm{span}(F)$ and the ambient standard basis: two bases of the same
   103		subspace form the rows of row-equivalent matrices, which have the same
   104		reduced row echelon form and hence the same pivot set $J$. The presentation
   105		through Gaussian elimination, adopted by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, makes the
   106		canonical complement efficiently computable. If $S$ is a register subspace
   107		spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the canonical complement of
   108		$\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its span coincides with
   109		$S^\perp$.
   110	\end{definition}
   111	
   112	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:canonical-complement}
   113		\uses{def:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   114		Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors
   115		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subseteq V$, let $F^\perp$ be the canonical
   116		complement of $F$, and let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. Then
   117		\[
   118			S + T = V\;, \qquad S \cap T = \{0\}\;.
   119		\]
   120	\end{lemma}
   121	\begin{proof}
   122		\uses{def:canonical-complement}
   123		Let $A = (a_{i,j})$ be the $m \times n$ matrix whose rows are the $v_i$ and
   124		write $A = UB$ with $U$ invertible and $B$ in reduced row echelon form, so
   125		that the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span $S$. The restrictions
   126		of the rows of $B$ to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   127		span $\F^m$, so for every $u \in V$ there is $v \in S$ that agrees with $u$
   128		on the coordinates in $J$. The difference $u - v$ is then supported on the
   129		coordinates outside $J$, that is, $u - v \in T$, which proves $S + T = V$.
   130		Counting dimensions forces $S \cap T = \{0\}$.
   131	\end{proof}
   132	
   133	\begin{definition}[Canonical linear map with prescribed kernel]\label{def:cl-canonical}
   134		\uses{def:canonical-complement, lem:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   135		Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors and let
   136		$F^\perp$ be its canonical complement. The \emph{canonical linear map
   137		$L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ with kernel basis $F$} is the projector onto $T$
   138		parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and
   139		$T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$; this is well defined by
   140		Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement}. Since the canonical complement
   141		depends only on $\mathrm{span}(F)$
   142		(Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}), so does $L$, and we also call
   143		it the \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$}. Note that
   144		$\ker(L) = S$.
   145	\end{definition}
   146	
   147	\begin{definition}[The map $L^\perp$]\label{def:Lperp}
   148		\uses{def:cl-canonical, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   149		Let $L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ be a linear map and let $F$ be a basis for
   150		$\ker(L)^\perp$. Define $L^\perp : V \to V$ as the canonical linear map with
   151		kernel basis $F$. (By the basis-independence noted in
   152		Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}, the map $L^\perp$ depends only
   153		on $\ker(L)$ and not on the chosen basis $F$.)
   154	\end{definition}

   525	\section{Generalized Pauli observables}
   526	% Paper label sec:generalized-pauli kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   527	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
   528	
   529	\begin{definition}[Generalized Pauli observables]\label{def:generalized-pauli}
   530		\uses{def:subfield-trace, def:lin-reg}
   531		Let $p$ be a prime and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$. The \emph{generalized Pauli
   532		observables over $\F_p$} are the unitaries on $\C^{\F_p}$ given by
   533		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-fp}
   534			\sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   535			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   536			\sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \omega^{bj} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   537		\end{equation}
   538		for $a, b \in \F_p$, with arithmetic over $\F_p$. For $q = p^k$, the
   539		\emph{generalized Pauli observables over $\F_q$} are the unitaries on
   540		$\C^{\F_q}$
   541		\[
   542			\tau^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   543			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   544			\tau^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \omega^{\tr(bj)} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   545		\]
   546		for $a, b \in \F_q$, where $\tr$ here denotes $\tr_{q \to p}$
   547		(Definition~\ref{def:subfield-trace}); for admissible $q$ this agrees with
   548		the standing shorthand, $p = 2$, and $\omega = -1$, so that all phases are
   549		signs. All the $\tau^X$ operators commute with one another, as do all the
   550		$\tau^Z$ operators. Their common eigenbases consist of the vectors
   551		$\ket{e_W}$, labeled by $e \in \F_q$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
   552		\[
   553			\ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{j \in \F_q}
   554			\omega^{-\tr(ej)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
   555			\ket{e_Z} = \ket{e}\;;
   556		\]
   557		the Fourier transform
   558		\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourier-f}
   559			F = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b \in \F_q}
   560			\omega^{-\tr(ab)} \ket{a}\bra{b}
   561		\end{equation}
   562		maps the computational ($Z$) eigenbasis to the $X$ eigenbasis. We write
   563		$\{\tau^W_e\}_{e \in \F_q}$ for the projective measurement whose elements
   564		are the rank-one projectors onto the vectors of the $W$ eigenbasis. For
   565		systems of $n$ qudits, we write, for $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a \in \F_q^n$,
   566		\[
   567			\tau^W(a) = \tau^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \tau^W(a_n)\;, \qquad
   568			\ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}
   569		\]
   570		for $e \in \F_q^n$, with associated rank-one projectors $\tau^W_e$.
   571	\end{definition}
   572	
   573	\begin{lemma}[Product and twisted commutation relations]\label{lem:twisted-commutation}
   574		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   575		Let $q = p^k$, let $n \ge 1$ be an integer, and let $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   576		\begin{enumerate}
   577			\item For all $a, a' \in \F_q$ and $b \in \F_p$,
   578			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
   579				      \tau^W(a)\, \tau^W(a') = \tau^W(a + a')
   580				      \qquad \text{and} \qquad
   581				      \bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^b = \tau^W(ab)\;;
   582			      \end{equation}
   583			      in particular $\bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^p = \Id$, so each
   584			      $\tau^W(a)$ is a unitary with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots
   585			      of unity.
   586			\item For all $a, b \in \F_q^n$,
   587			      % Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   588			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fq}
   589				      \tau^X(a)\, \tau^Z(b)
   590				      = \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)}\, \tau^Z(b)\, \tau^X(a)\;,
   591			      \end{equation}
   592			      where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i \in \F_q$. The case
   593			      $q = p$, $n = 1$ reads
   594			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fp}
   595				      \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b)
   596				      = \omega^{-ab}\, \sigma^Z(b)\, \sigma^X(a)
   597				      \qquad \text{for all } a, b \in \F_p\;.
   598			      \end{equation}
   599		\end{enumerate}
   600	\end{lemma}
   601	\begin{proof}
   602		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}
   603		All identities are verified on computational basis states. For the product
   604		relations with $W = X$, shifting twice by $a'$ and $a$ equals shifting by
   605		$a + a'$; with $W = Z$, the phases $\omega^{\tr(aj)}\omega^{\tr(a'j)}$
   606		combine by $\F_q$-linearity of the trace, and the power relation follows by
   607		iterating. For the scalar twisted commutation,
   608		$\tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$, while
   609		$\tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(b(j+a))}\ket{j + a} =
   610		\omega^{\tr(ab)}\,\omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$. The multi-qudit relation
   611		follows by applying the scalar relation factor by factor and summing the
   612		exponents, using $\tr(a \cdot b) = \sum_i \tr(a_i b_i)$. For $q = p$ the
   613		trace is the identity map, which gives \eqref{eq:twisted-fp}.
   614	\end{proof}
   615	
   616	\begin{lemma}[Fourier cancellation over a subspace]\label{lem:cancellation}
   617		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal, def:subfield-trace}
   618		Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_q^k$ and let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$, where
   619		$p$ is the characteristic of $\F_q$ and $\tr = \tr_{q \to p}$. For all
   620		$v \notin V^\perp$,
   621		\[
   622			\E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr(\bu \cdot v)} = 0\;,
   623		\]
   624		where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $\bu$ in $V$.
   625	\end{lemma}
   626	\begin{proof}
   627		This is Fact 3.2 of \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Since $v \notin V^\perp$,
   628		the $\F_q$-linear functional $u \mapsto u \cdot v$ is not identically zero
   629		on $V$, hence surjective onto $\F_q$; composing with the nonzero map $\tr$
   630		shows that there is $u_0 \in V$ with $\tr(u_0 \cdot v) \neq 0$. Writing $C$
   631		for the expectation, translation invariance of the uniform distribution on
   632		$V$ gives
   633		$C = \E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr((\bu + u_0) \cdot v)}
   634		= \omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)}\, C$, and $\omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)} \neq 1$
   635		forces $C = 0$.
   636	\end{proof}
   637	
   638	\begin{lemma}[Fourier expansion of Pauli observables]\label{lem:pauli-observable-expansion}
   639		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}
   640		For every integer $n \ge 1$, all $W \in \{X, Z\}$, and all $a \in \F_q^n$,
   641		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   642		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj}
   643			\tau^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \F_q^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}\, \tau^W_b\;,
   644		\end{equation}
   645		and conversely
   646		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
   647			\E_{\ba \sim \F_q^n}\, \omega^{-\tr(\ba \cdot b)}\, \tau^W(\ba)
   648			= \sum_{b' \in \F_q^n} \E_{\ba \sim \F_q^n}\,
   649			\omega^{\tr(\ba \cdot (b' - b))}\, \tau^W_{b'}
   650			= \tau^W_b\;.
   651		\end{equation}
   652	\end{lemma}
   653	\begin{proof}
   654		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, lem:cancellation}
   655		Each $\ket{b_W}$ is an eigenvector of $\tau^W(a)$ with eigenvalue
   656		$\omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}$: for $W = Z$ this is immediate from the
   657		definition, and for $W = X$ it follows from the single-qudit computation
   658		$\tau^X(a)\ket{e_X} = \omega^{\tr(ae)}\ket{e_X}$, applied factor by factor.
   659		Expanding $\tau^W(a)$ in the orthonormal eigenbasis
   660		$\{\ket{b_W}\}_{b \in \F_q^n}$ gives the first display. For the inversion,
   661		substitute the first display and exchange the order of summation; by
   662		Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation} applied with $V = \F_q^n$ (so that
   663		$V^\perp = \{0\}$), the inner expectation vanishes unless $b' = b$, where
   664		it equals $1$.
   665	\end{proof}

   441	\section{Conditionally linear functions and distributions}
   442	% Paper subsection label sec:cl kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   443	\label{sec:cl}
   444	
   445	Conditionally linear functions specify the question distributions of the games considered in the following chapters in a form that can be ``introspected''. Intuitively, a conditionally linear function takes as input an element $x \in V = \F^n$ and applies linear maps $L_j$ sequentially to $x^{V_j}$, where $V_1, V_2, \dots$ is a sequence of complementary register subspaces such that both the linear map $L_j$ and the subspace $V_j$, for $j \ge 2$, may depend on the values taken by the previous linear maps $L_1(x^{V_1})$, $L_2(x^{V_2})$, and so on.
   446	
   447	Throughout this section $V$ denotes the linear space $\F^n$ for some integer $n \ge 0$, and all the distinguished subspaces of $V$ are register subspaces (Definition~\ref{def:register-subspace}).    448	\[
   449		V_{<k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\,1 \le j < k} V_j\,, \qquad V_{>k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\,\ell \ge j > k} V_j\,,
   450	\]
   451	and $V_{\le k}$, $V_{\ge k}$ are understood to be $V_{<k+1}$ and $V_{>k-1}$, respectively. For a register subspace $V'$ of $V$, the symbol $x^{V'}$ denotes the projection of $x$ onto $V'$ parallel to the complementary register subspace (Definition~\ref{def:complementary}). Moreover, if $F \colon V' \to V'$ is a function and $x \in V$, we write $x^F$ for $F(x^{V'})$; for example, in the following definition $x^{L_1}$ is shorthand for $L_1(x^{V_1})$.
   452	
   453	\begin{definition}[Conditionally linear functions]\label{def:cl-func}
   454		\uses{def:register-subspace, def:complementary}
   455		Let $V$ be $\F^n$ for some $n \ge 0$. For all integers $\ell \ge 0$ the collection of \emph{$\ell$-level conditionally linear functions} (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is defined inductively as follows.
   456		\begin{enumerate}
   457			\item There is a single $0$-level conditionally linear function, which is the $0$ function on $V$.
   458			\item Let $\ell \ge 1$ and suppose the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear functions has been defined. The collection of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions on $V$ consists of all functions $L$ on $V$ that can be expressed in the following form: there exist complementary register subspaces $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ of $V$, a linear function $L_1$ on $V_1$, and, for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$, an $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear function $L_{>1,\,v}$ on $V_{>1}$, such that for all $x \in V$,
   459			\[
   460				L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{V_{>1}})\,.
   461			\]
   462		\end{enumerate}
   463	\end{definition}
   464	
   465	We abbreviate ``conditionally linear'' as \emph{CL}. Operationally, an $\ell$-level CL function first applies $L_1$ to $x^{V_1}$; conditioned on the value $x^{L_1}$ it selects a register subspace $V_2$ and a linear map $L_2$ and applies $L_2$ to $x^{V_2}$; and so on, finally outputting $\sum_{k=1}^{\ell} x^{L_k}$. Every $1$-level CL function is linear, and conversely every linear map on $V$ is a $1$-level CL function. Moreover, for every $\ell \ge 1$ the collection of $\ell$-level CL functions contains the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level CL functions.
   466	
   467	\begin{definition}[Conditionally linear distributions]\label{def:cl-dist}
   468		\uses{def:cl-func}
   469		Let $L, R \colon V \to V$ be conditionally linear functions. The \emph{conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ corresponding to $(L,R)$} is the distribution over pairs $(L(x), R(x)) \in V \times V$ for $x$ drawn uniformly at random from $V$.
   470	\end{definition}
   471	
   472	Note that both players' questions are generated from the \emph{same} uniformly random seed $x$; this shared-seed structure is what the introspection technique exploits. The following lemma elucidates the structural properties of $\ell$-level CL functions. Recall that $x^{L_{<k}}$ and $x^{L_k}$ denote $L_{<k}(x)$ and $L_{k,\,u}(x^{V_{k,\,u}})$ where $u = L_{<k}(x)$.
   473	
   474	\begin{lemma}[Structure of conditionally linear functions]\label{lem:cl-kth}
   475		\uses{def:cl-func, def:register-subspace}
   476		Let $\ell \ge 1$ and $V = \F^n$ for some integer $n \ge 0$. A function $L \colon V \to V$ is an $\ell$-level CL function if and only if the following collection of functions and subspaces exists:
   477		\begin{enumerate}
   478			\item[(i)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$, a function $L_{\le k} \colon V \to V$, called the \emph{$k$-th marginal of $L$};
   479			\item[(ii)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{<k}(V)$, a register subspace $V_{k,\,u}$ of $V$, called the \emph{$k$-th factor space with prefix $u$};
   480			\item[(iii)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{<k}(V)$, a linear map $L_{k,\,u} \colon V_{k,\,u} \to V_{k,\,u}$, called the \emph{$k$-th linear map of $L$ with prefix $u$};
   481		\end{enumerate}
   482		such that the following conditions hold for all $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$:
   483		\begin{enumerate}

   485			\item $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell} V_{i,\,x^{L_{<i}}}$ for all $x \in V$;
   486			\item $L_{\le k}(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} x^{L_i}$ for all $x \in V$, where $L_i$ is shorthand notation for $L_{i,\,x^{L_{<i}}}$;
   487			\item $L = L_{\le \ell}$.

There are $6$ linear equations over these variables: for each of the three rows and each of the first two columns, the sum of the three variables in it equals $0$; for the third column, the sum of the three variables in it equals $1$.
   191	
   192		The question types are
   193		\begin{align*}
   194			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} &= \{\mathsf{Constraint}_i : i = 1,2,\ldots,6\}\;,\\
   195			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}} &= \{\mathsf{Variable}_j : j = 1,2,\ldots,9\}\;,\\
   196			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ms}} &= \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} \cup \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}\;,
   197		\end{align*}

   199	
   200		The question distribution is as follows: the verifier samples $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ uniformly from $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}}$, then samples $\mathsf{Variable}_j$ uniformly among the three variables appearing in the row or column of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$; one player, chosen uniformly at random, receives $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and the other receives $\mathsf{Variable}_j$.    188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal

   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}

   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}

   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.

   320	\paragraph{Decision procedure} The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the
   321	game $\game^\ld$ is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}.
   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.
   412	
   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
   415	  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}
   425	      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
   426	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   427	      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
   428	      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
   429	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   430				 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
   431	      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
   432	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   433	      G^\bob_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}\;,
   434	    \end{split}
   435	  \end{equation*}
   436	  where $\delta_{\ld} = \delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc)$, 
   437	  and all three statements are with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$.
   438	In addition, the first two approximations hold under the uniform distribution over $u\in \F_q^m$,
   439		whereas there is no question distribution associated with the third approximation.
   440	\end{theorem}
   441	
   442	\begin{proof}
   443	Let $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
   444	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
   445	and $m$ divides $q$. Let $\Sigma=\F_q$. Let $\code \subseteq \Sigma^q$ be the Reed-Solomon code with degree $d$. Explicitly, $\code$ is the set of all $(p(x_1),\ldots,p(x_n))$ where $p:\F_q\to\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are an enumeration of $\F_q$. Then in the (standard) notation from~\cite{ji2021quantum} $\code$ is a linear $[q,d+1,n-d+1]_\Sigma$ code.
   446	
   447	Observe that the two-prover tensor code test, for the code $\code^{\otimes m}$, as described in~\cite[Figure 1 and Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}, is identical to the game $\game^\ld$ with parameters $\ldparams$ and $\ldc=1$, whose decider is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}. This is because 
   448	\begin{enumerate}
   449	\item The \emph{axis-parallel line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{axis-parallel lines test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with the only difference that in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} the roles of A and B are chosen uniformly at random. This is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor code test from~\cite[Section 4.1]{ji2021quantum}.
   450	\item The \emph{diagonal line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{subcube commutation test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with again the added symmetrization between players. 
   451	\item The \emph{consistency test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{synchronicity test} from~\cite[Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}.
   452	\end{enumerate}
   453	
   454	As a result,~\cite[Theorem 4.7]{ji2021quantum}, in which we choose the parameter $k$ as $k=m^3d$,  immediately yields \Cref{lem:ld-soundness}.
   455	
   456	To conclude it remains to extend the result to the case of general $\ldc$. This is done 
   457	via a standard reduction, following exactly the same steps as the derivation of Theorem 4.43 from Theorem 4.40 in~\cite{NW19}.
   458	\end{proof}

   465	\subsubsection{Complexity of the classical low-degree test.}
   466	The CL functions and decision procedure of the low-degree test are incorporated
   467	as subroutines in some of the normal form verifiers constructed in subsequent
   468	sections.
   469	The next lemma establishes the time complexity of these procedures as a function
   470	of the parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$.
   471	The lemma also establishes the time complexity of computing the {description} of
   472	the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ as a Turing machine, given the parameter
   473	tuple $\ldparams$ as input.
   474	
   475	
   476	
   477	\begin{lemma}[Complexity of the classical low-degree test]
   478	  \label{lem:ld-complexity}
   479	  Let $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$ denote a parameter tuple.
   480	  \begin{enumerate}
   481		\item The time complexity of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$
   482	    parametrized by $\ldparams$ is $\poly(m, d, k, \log q)$.
   483		\item The time complexity of evaluating marginals of the CL functions
   484	    $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$, and $L_\DLine$ at a given input point is $\poly(m, \log
   485	    q)$.
   486		\item The Turing machine description of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$
   487	    parametrized by $\ldparams$ can be computed from $\ldparams$ in $\polylog
   488	    (q,m,d,k)$ time.
   489	  \end{enumerate}
   490	\end{lemma}
   491	
   492	\begin{proof}
   493		Finite field arithmetic over $\F_q$ can be performed in time $\polylog q$, by
   494	  Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}.
   495		The most expensive step in $\decider^\ld$ is to evaluate a univariate
   496	  polynomial $f: \F_q \to \F_q^k$ at some point $t_u \in \F_q$ that corresponds
   497	  to a point $u \in \F_q^m$, which takes time $\poly(m,d,k,\log q)$.
   498	  The function $L_\Point$ is a projection onto $V_\xpt$, which takes time
   499	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ to compute (it just involves ``zeroing out'' the registers
   500	  outside of $V_\xpt$).

     6	This chapter defines the two testing primitives underlying the question-reduction step: the \emph{classical low individual degree game}, in its simultaneous form, and the \emph{Pauli basis test}, a nonlocal game built from the classical game together with the Magic Square game. The chapter closes with the qubit form of the soundness statement (Corollary~\ref{cor:pauli-binary}) and the canonical parameter choice with its soundness bound (Definition~\ref{def:introparams}, Lemma~\ref{lem:delta-bound}).

    10	\section{The classical low individual degree game}
    11	% Paper labels sec:ld-verifier and sec:ld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
    12	\label{sec:ld-verifier}
    13	\label{sec:ld-game}
    14	
    15	The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.

    17	\begin{definition}[The classical low individual degree game: parameters and registers]\label{def:ld-game}
    18		\uses{def:game, def:admissible-size}
    19		% The source fixes \N to be the set of positive integers
    20		% (references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:6) and takes m, d, ldc in \N
    21		% (references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:33-35),
    22		% so the positivity below is the source's implicit domain, stated explicitly.
    23		% It is load-bearing: at d = 0 or k = 0 the prefactor a(dmk)^a of delta_ld in
    24		% lem:ld-soundness vanishes, and at d = 0 the resulting exact conclusions fail

    27		The game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ is parametrized by a tuple $\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$, where $m, d, k \ge 1$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}), and $m$ divides $q$.     28		\[
    29			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}} = \{\mathsf{Point}, \mathsf{ALine}, \mathsf{DLine}\}\;,
    30		\]
    31		and the distribution over type pairs $(t_{\mathrm A}, t_{\mathrm B})$ is uniform over $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}} \times \mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}}$. The ambient space is the direct sum $V = V_X \oplus V_I \oplus V_V$ of three register subspaces: the \emph{point register} $V_X \cong \F_q^m$, the \emph{coordinate register} $V_I \cong \F_q$, and the \emph{direction register} $V_V \cong \F_q^m$. Elements of $V$ are identified with triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times \F_q^m$. The question distribution and the win predicate of $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ are specified in Definitions~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} and~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} below.
    32	\end{definition}

    34	\begin{definition}[Question distribution of the classical low individual degree game]\label{def:ld-question-distribution}
    35		\uses{def:ld-game, def:cl-func, def:cl-dist, lem:cl-concat, def:cl-canonical, def:line-representative}
    36		Let $\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ be as in Definition~\ref{def:ld-game}. Define $L_{\mathsf{Point}}$ to be the $1$-level CL function on $V$ that projects onto $V_X$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
    37		\begin{equation}
    38			\label{eq:cl-ptf}
    39			L_{\mathsf{Point}}(u,s,v) = (u,0,0)\;.
    40		\end{equation}
    41		For $s \in \F_q$, let $\chi(s)$ be the unique integer such that
    42		\begin{equation}
    43			\label{eq:chi-func}
    44			s = (\chi(s)-1)\,\frac{q}{m} + r
    45		\end{equation}
    46		for some $0 \le r < q/m$, where $s$ is interpreted as an integer in $\{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}$ under the identification of $\F_q$ with binary strings fixed in Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}.     47		\begin{equation}
    48			\label{eq:cl-alnf}
    49			L_{\mathsf{ALine}}(u,s,v) = \bigl(L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u),\, s,\, 0\bigr)\quad\text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V\;,
    50		\end{equation}
    51		where $i = \chi(s)$ and $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ denotes the canonical linear map with one-dimensional kernel spanned by $v$, used to compute canonical representatives of lines (Definition~\ref{def:line-representative}). Define $L_{\mathsf{DLine}}$ by
    52		\begin{equation}
    53			\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
    54			L_{\mathsf{DLine}}(u,s,v) = \bigl(L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),\, s,\, \pi_{i-1}(v)\bigr)\;,
    55		\end{equation}

    58		The question distribution of $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ is the typed CL distribution obtained as follows: sample a type pair $(t_{\mathrm A}, t_{\mathrm B})$ uniformly from $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}} \times \mathcal T^{\mathrm{ld}}$, sample $z = (u,s,v)$ uniformly from $V$, and send each player $w \in \{\mathrm A,\mathrm B\}$ the question $(t_w, L_{t_w}(z))$.

    61	The next two lemmas show that the CL functions $L_{\mathsf{Point}}$, $L_{\mathsf{ALine}}$, $L_{\mathsf{DLine}}$ give rise to the axis-parallel and diagonal line-versus-point distributions.

    63	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:alnf}
    64		\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}
    65		Consider the pair $(\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\bigl((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0)\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_{\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\ell = \ell(u_0, e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.     66	\end{lemma}
    67	\begin{proof}
    68		\uses{def:line-representative}

    72	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:dlnf}
    73		\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}
    74		Consider the pair $(\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\bigl((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0)\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_{\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\ell = \ell(u_0, v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.     82		\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, lem:alnf, lem:dlnf}
    83		The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the distribution $\mu_{L_{\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\ell = (u_0,e_i),\, u)$, where we omit the $0$ components for simplicity.     86	\begin{definition}[Win predicate of the classical low individual degree game]\label{def:ld-win-predicate}
    87		\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:line, def:polyfunc}
    88		Fix $\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$. Answers in the game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}_{\mathsf{ldparams}}$ take the following forms, depending on the question type; answers not of the prescribed form are rejected.
    89		\begin{itemize}
    90			\item Type $\mathsf{Point}$, question content $u \in \F_q^m$: the answer is an element of $\F_q^k$.
    91			\item Type $\mathsf{ALine}$, question content $(u_0,s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$, specifying the axis-parallel line $\ell(u_0,e_i)$ with $i = \chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple $(f_1,\ldots,f_k)$ of univariate polynomials $f_j\colon \F_q \to \F_q$ of degree at most $d$, each given by its $d+1$ coefficients.

   107	\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}
   108		The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, so any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount; the game-correspondence obligation enumerated in the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} accounts for this event explicitly, and an error of this shape is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.
   109	\end{remark}

   113	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]\label{def:ld-meas}
   114		\uses{def:polyfunc, def:polymeasurements, def:polynomials-degree}
   115		Let $\polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ denote the set of POVM measurements indexed by $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, the polynomial representatives of individual degree at most $d$ in each variable; this is the notion of Definition~\ref{def:polymeasurements}, and the argument order $(m,q,d)$ follows that definition (the paper orders the arguments as $(m,d,q)$).    170		In this regime the statement is imported, and the source's route is as follows: identify the game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}_{\mathsf{ldparams}}$ with $k = 1$ with the two-prover tensor-code test for the code $\code^{\ot m}$ of~\cite{Ji2021Quantum} (Figures~1 and~2 there, the roles of the two players being assigned uniformly at random); apply Theorem~4.7 of~\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, instantiated with its auxiliary integer parameter --- denoted $k$ there and unrelated to the simultaneity parameter $k$ of $\mathsf{ldparams}$ --- chosen as $m^3 d$, so that its error function $\mathrm{poly}(m, d+1, m^3d) \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\eps, q^{-1}, e^{-md})$ takes the displayed form of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$; and extend from $k = 1$ to general $k$ by a standard reduction, following exactly the derivation of Theorem~4.43 from Theorem~4.40 in~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. The import carries two verification obligations, which remain open; they are enumerated here as obligations and detailed, together with candidate repairs, in the import-obligations section of~\cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}.
   171		\begin{enumerate}
   172			\item (\emph{Game correspondence.}) The source asserts that the two games are identical; they are not. In the cited test, the subcube commutation and pair-synchronicity branches send an ordered pair of points of a \emph{hidden} subcube and receive a pair of field values --- a question type that $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ does not have --- its line questions carry no analogue of the seed $s$, its nontrivial cross-tests have mass $1/3$ where the present ones have $2/9$, and it fixes no acceptance convention on the zero-direction event of Remark~\ref{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}, whose probability is at most $\frac1m \sum_{j=1}^m q^{-j} \le \frac{1}{m(q-1)} \le \frac{2}{mq}$ over uniform $(s,v)$.    263	\section{The Pauli basis test}
   264	% Paper label sec:qld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   265	\label{sec:qld-game}
   266	
   267	The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.

  1074	The CL functions corresponding to the Pauli basis test question distribution are
  1075	parameterized by the parameter tuple $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$.

  1077	\times (\F_q)^2$.
  1078	The space $V^\pauli$ is decomposed into a direct sum of the following register
  1079	subspaces: $V_\xpt,V_\zpt$ (which are $m$-dimensional), $V_\coord$ (which is
  1080	$1$-dimensional), $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is $m$-dimensional), and
  1081	$V_{\rxpt},V_{\rzpt}$ (which are $1$-dimensional).
  1082	We identify elements of $V^\pauli$ as tuples $(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1083	\in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m \times (\F_q)^2$.

  1085	\in \type^\pauli$:

  1088	  = L_\Point(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\Point$ is the $1$-level CL function defined in
  1089	  \Cref{eq:cl-ptf}.\footnote{The range $V_{\xpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus
  1090	    V_{\dir{}}$ or $V_{\zpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ of $L_\Point$ is
  1091	    embedded in $V^\pauli$ in the natural way.
  1092	    The same convention is used also in Item 2 and 3 for $L_\ALine$ and
  1093	    $L_\DLine$.}
  1094	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\ALine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1095	  = L_\ALine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\ALine$ is the $2$-level CL function defined in
  1096	  \Cref{eq:cl-alnf}.
  1097	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\DLine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)

  1102	  (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,0,0,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$, i.e., it projects onto $V_\xpt \oplus

   263	\section{The Pauli basis test}
   264	% Paper label sec:qld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   265	\label{sec:qld-game}
   266	
   267	The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.

   331	\begin{definition}[Win predicate of the Pauli basis test]\label{def:pauli-win-predicate}
   332		\uses{def:pauli-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ms-game, def:indicator-vector, def:admissible}
   333		Fix an admissible tuple $\mathsf{qldparams} = (q,m,d)$ (Definition~\ref{def:admissible}) and let $M = 2^m$. Answers in the game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{\mathsf{qldparams}}$ take the following forms, depending on the question type; answers not of the prescribed form are rejected.
   334		% The paper's format table writes the line contents loosely as (u_W, s) and (u_W, s, v);
   335		% by the sampling procedure the actual contents are the canonical pairs (u_0, s) and
   336		% triples (u_0, s, v') with v' = pi_{i-1}(v). We state the canonical form.
   337		\begin{itemize}
   338			\item $(\mathsf{Point},W)$: content $y \in \F_q^m$; answer an element of $\F_q$.
   339			\item $(\mathsf{ALine},W)$: content $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$; answer a univariate polynomial $f\colon \F_q \to \F_q$ of degree at most $d$.
   340			\item $(\mathsf{DLine},W)$: content $(u_0, s, v') \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times \F_q^m$; answer a univariate polynomial $f\colon \F_q \to \F_q$ of degree at most $md$.
   341			\item $\mathsf{Pair}$: content $\omega = (u_X, u_Z, r_X, r_Z) \in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q^2$; answer $(\beta_X, \beta_Z) \in \F_2^2$.
   342			\item $(\mathsf{Pair},W)$: content $\omega$ as above; answer an element of $\F_2$.
   343			\item $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$: content $\omega$ as above; answer $(\alpha_{v_1}, \alpha_{v_2}, \alpha_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$, indexed by the variable indices $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$.
   344			\item $\mathsf{Variable}_j$: content $\omega$ as above; answer an element of $\F_2$.
   345			\item $(\mathsf{Pauli},W)$: content $0$; answer an element of $\F_q^M$.
   346		\end{itemize}
   347		The win predicate $D^{\mathrm{pauli}} = D^{\mathrm{pauli}}_{\mathsf{qldparams}}$ is the function of the tuple $(t_{\mathrm A}, x_{\mathrm A}, t_{\mathrm B}, x_{\mathrm B}, a_{\mathrm A}, a_{\mathrm B})$ determined by the following clauses, evaluated for $w \in \{\mathrm A, \mathrm B\}$ and $W \in \{X,Z\}$; in all cases where no action is indicated, the predicate accepts. In the last four clauses, the content of the player whose type lies in $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ms}} \cup \{\mathsf{Pair}, (\mathsf{Pair},X), (\mathsf{Pair},Z)\}$ is a tuple $(u_X, u_Z, r_X, r_Z)$, from which the predicate first computes
   348		\begin{equation}
   349			\label{eq:gamma-value}
   350			\gamma = \tr\bigl( (\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X) \cdot r_X) \cdot (\mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \bigr) \in \F_2\;,
   351		\end{equation}
   352		where $\mathrm{ind}_m(\cdot) \in \F_q^M$ is the indicator vector of the low-degree encoding (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}), the inner dot denotes the dot product on $\F_q^M$, and $\tr\colon \F_q \to \F_2$ is the finite-field trace.
   353		\begin{enumerate}
   354			\item (\textbf{Consistency check}) If $t_{\mathrm A} = t_{\mathrm B}$, accept if and only if $a_{\mathrm A} = a_{\mathrm B}$.
   355			\item (\textbf{Low-degree check}) Let $\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,1)$; admissibility of $\mathsf{qldparams}$ gives $d \ge 1$ and $m \mid q$, so this is a parameter tuple as in Definition~\ref{def:ld-game}.
   356			\begin{enumerate}
   357				\item If $t_w = (\mathsf{Point},W)$ and $t_{\overline w} = (\mathsf{ALine},W)$, accept if $D^{\mathrm{ld}}_{\mathsf{ldparams}}$ accepts $(\mathsf{Point}, x_w, \mathsf{ALine}, x_{\overline w}, a_w, a_{\overline w})$.
   358				\item If $t_w = (\mathsf{Point},W)$ and $t_{\overline w} = (\mathsf{DLine},W)$, accept if $D^{\mathrm{ld}}_{\mathsf{ldparams}}$ accepts $(\mathsf{Point}, x_w, \mathsf{DLine}, x_{\overline w}, a_w, a_{\overline w})$.
   359			\end{enumerate}
   360			\item (\textbf{Consistency check}) If $t_w = (\mathsf{Point},W)$ and $t_{\overline w} = (\mathsf{Pauli},W)$, accept if $g_{a_{\overline w}}(x_w) = a_w$, where $g_{a_{\overline w}}$ is the low-degree encoding of $a_{\overline w} \in \F_q^M$ (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}).
   361			\item (\textbf{Commutation check}) If $t_w = (\mathsf{Pair},W)$ and $t_{\overline w} = \mathsf{Pair}$, accept if $a_w = \beta_W$ or $\gamma \neq 0$.
   362			\item (\textbf{Consistency check}) If $t_w = (\mathsf{Point},W)$ and $t_{\overline w} = (\mathsf{Pair},W)$, accept if $\tr(a_w r_W) = a_{\overline w}$ or $\gamma \neq 0$.
   363			\item (\textbf{Magic Square check}) If $t_w = \mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and $t_{\overline w} = \mathsf{Variable}_j$, accept if $\gamma = 0$, or if $a_w$ satisfies the equation of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and $\alpha_j = a_{\overline w}$.
   364			\item (\textbf{Consistency check}) If $t_w = (\mathsf{Point},W)$ and $t_{\overline w} = \mathsf{Variable}_j$, accept if $\gamma = 0$, or if $j = 1$, $W = X$, and $\tr(a_w r_X) = a_{\overline w}$, or if $j = 5$, $W = Z$, and $\tr(a_w r_Z) = a_{\overline w}$.
   365		\end{enumerate}
   366		The game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{\mathsf{qldparams}}$ is the typed game with type set $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{pauli}}$, the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:pauli-question-distribution}, and win predicate $D^{\mathrm{pauli}}_{\mathsf{qldparams}}$.
   367	\end{definition}
   368	
   369	Note the one-sided gating on $\gamma$: the commutation check and the $\mathsf{Pair}$ consistency check accept automatically when $\gamma \neq 0$, while the Magic Square check and the $\mathsf{Variable}$ consistency check accept automatically when $\gamma = 0$.

    10	\begin{definition}[POVMs, sub-measurements, and observables]\label{def:povm-conventions}
    11		\uses{def:submeasurement}

    15		Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued measures (POVMs). A \emph{POVM} on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ is a family of positive semidefinite operators $\{M_a\}_{a \in S}$ indexed by outcomes $a$ ranging over a finite set $S$ such that $\sum_a M_a = \Id$; if the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \le \Id$, then $\{M_a\}$ is a \emph{sub-measurement}.     16		\[
    17			\Prb(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\,.
    18		\]
    19		A POVM $M = \{M_a\}$ is \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$); this automatically implies that $M_a M_b = M_b M_a = 0$ for distinct outcomes $a \ne b$.     22		\[
    23			M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\,b}\,, \qquad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\,b}\,;
    24		\]

    47	\section{Games and strategies}
    48	% Paper subsection label sec:strat kept for cross-reference fidelity.
    49	\label{sec:strat}

    51	\begin{definition}[Two-player one-round games]\label{def:game}
    52		A \emph{two-player one-round game} $\mathfrak G$ is specified by a tuple $(\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ where
    53		\begin{enumerate}
    54			\item $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ are finite sets, called the \emph{question alphabets},
    55			\item $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ are finite sets, called the \emph{answer alphabets},
    56			\item $\mu$ is a probability distribution over $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$, called the \emph{question distribution}, and
    57			\item $D \colon \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \times \mathcal A \times \mathcal B \to \{0,1\}$ is a function, called the \emph{decision predicate}.
    58		\end{enumerate}
    59	\end{definition}
    60	
    61	\begin{definition}[Tensor product strategies]\label{def:tensor-product-strategy}
    62		\uses{def:game, def:povm-conventions}
    63		A \emph{tensor product strategy} $\mathcal S$ for a game $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ is a tuple $(\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ where
    64		\begin{itemize}
    65			\item $\ket{\psi}$ is a pure quantum state, i.e.\ a unit vector in $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ for finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_A$, $\mathcal H_B$,
    66			\item $A$ is a set $\{A^x\}$ such that for every $x \in \mathcal X$, $A^x = \{A^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ is a POVM on $\mathcal H_A$, and
    67			\item $B$ is a set $\{B^y\}$ such that for every $y \in \mathcal Y$, $B^y = \{B^y_b\}_{b \in \mathcal B}$ is a POVM on $\mathcal H_B$.
    68		\end{itemize}
    69	\end{definition}
    70	
    71	\begin{definition}[Tensor product value]\label{def:tensor-product-value}
    72		\uses{def:tensor-product-strategy}
    73		The \emph{tensor product value} of a tensor product strategy $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ with respect to a game $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ is
    74		\[
    75			\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S) = \sum_{x,\,y,\,a,\,b} \mu(x,y)\, D(x,y,a,b)\, \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^y_b \ket{\psi}\,.
    76		\]
    77		For $v \in [0,1]$ we say that the strategy $\mathcal S$ \emph{passes (or wins) $\mathfrak G$ with probability $v$} if $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S) \ge v$. The \emph{tensor product value} of $\mathfrak G$ is
    78		\[
    79			\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G) = \sup_{\mathcal S} \operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S)\,,
    80		\]
    81		where the supremum is taken over all tensor product strategies $\mathcal S$ for $\mathfrak G$.
    82	\end{definition}

   173	\begin{definition}[Distance between states]\label{def:state-distance}
   174		Let $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}_{n \in \N}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}_{n \in \N}$ be two families of states in the same space $\mathcal H$. For a function $\delta \colon \N \to [0,1]$ we say that $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-close}, denoted $\ket{\psi} \approx_\delta \ket{\psi'}$, if
   175		\[
   176			\lVert \ket{\psi_n} - \ket{\psi'_n} \rVert^2 = O(\delta(n))\,.
   177		\]
   178		The dependence of the states and of $\delta$ on the indexing parameter $n$ is generally left implicit; we write, e.g., $\ket{\psi}$ for $\ket{\psi_n}$.
   179	\end{definition}
   180	
   181	\begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]\label{def:consistency}
   182		\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
   183		Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ be a quantum state, and for all $x \in \mathcal X$ let $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ be POVMs. We write
   184		\[
   185			A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a
   186		\]
   187		on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
   188		\[
   189			\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_{a \ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^x_b \ket{\psi} = O(\delta)\,.
   190		\]
   191		In this case we say that $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-consistent} on $\ket{\psi}$. As in Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}, the $O(\cdot)$ refers to families of POVMs and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n \in \N$, and is taken as $n \to \infty$.
   192	\end{definition}
   193	
   194	A measurement that is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement} is $0$-consistent with itself on the same state under the singleton distribution, and vice versa: if $\sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \ot M_a \ket{\psi} = 1$, then $M_a \ot \Id\, \ket{\psi} = \Id \ot M_a\, \ket{\psi}$ for every $a$, by the equality case of the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality applied outcome by outcome.
   195	
   196	% The source (references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:257-274) states this
   197	% definition for pairs of POVMs but applies the relation to arbitrary operator families:
   198	% to plain operators at 06:313-330, to sets of matrices at 06:364-380, and to products and
   199	% commutators, compared against the zero family, at 06:409-445. The general form below,
   200	% for arbitrary finite families of operators, is the one of the NEEXP source
   201	% (references/neexp-paper/05_quantum_preliminaries.tex:385-391), from which the distance
   202	% calculus is imported; the POVM case is singled out after the display.
   203	\begin{definition}[State-dependent distance between operator families]\label{def:povm-distance}
   204		\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
   205		Let $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal A$ be finite sets and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H$ be a quantum state, and for all $x \in \mathcal X$ let $\{M^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ and $\{N^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ be two families of linear operators on $\mathcal H$. We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
   206		\[
   207			\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_a \lVert (M^x_a - N^x_a)\, \ket{\psi} \rVert^2 \le O(\delta)\,,
   208		\]
   209		and we write $M^x_a \approx_\delta N^x_a$ to denote this when the state $\ket{\psi}$ and the distribution $\mu$ are clear from context. This distance is referred to as the \emph{state-dependent} distance. The principal case is that in which $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are POVMs on $\mathcal H$, and we then speak of the state-dependent distance between the POVMs; but the relation is used for arbitrary operator families --- for instance for products of measurement operators, or for commutators compared against the identically zero family, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:commutation-analysis} below.
   210	\end{definition}
   211	
   212	\begin{definition}[Distance between strategies]\label{def:strategy-distance}
   213		\uses{def:tensor-product-strategy, def:state-distance, def:povm-distance}
   214		Let $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ be a nonlocal game and let $\mathcal S = (\psi, A, B)$ and $\mathcal S' = (\psi', A', B')$ be strategies for $\mathfrak G$. For $\delta \in [0,1]$ we say that \emph{$\mathcal S$ is $\delta$-close to $\mathcal S'$} if the following conditions hold.
   215		\begin{enumerate}
   216			\item The states $\ket{\psi}, \ket{\psi'}$ are states in the same Hilbert space $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ and are $\delta$-close.
   217			\item For all $x \in \mathcal X$ and $y \in \mathcal Y$, we have $A^x_a \approx_\delta (A')^x_a$ and $B^y_b \approx_\delta (B')^y_b$, with the approximations holding under the distribution $\mu$ (i.e.\ under its corresponding marginals), on either $\ket{\psi}$ or $\ket{\psi'}$.
   218		\end{enumerate}
   219	\end{definition}
   220	
   221	\begin{remark}[Asymptotic reading of the distance relations]\label{rem:asymptotic-distance}
   222		Definitions~\ref{def:state-distance}, \ref{def:consistency}, and \ref{def:povm-distance} are asymptotic: every $\approx_\delta$ and $\simeq_\delta$ statement refers to families of states and measurement families indexed by an implicit parameter $n \in \N$, and the $O(\cdot)$ is taken as $n \to \infty$. None of these relations is a pointwise inequality with an explicit constant. By contrast, the corresponding relations used in the low individual degree chapters (Definitions~\ref{def:simeq} and~\ref{def:approx_delta}) carry no hidden constant. Any explicit quantitative version of the present relations therefore retains the constants absorbed into the $O(\cdot)$; for instance, the triangle inequality of Lemma~\ref{fact:triangle} carries a factor $2$ inside the $O(\cdot)$.
   223	\end{remark}

     7	\subsection{Games and strategies}
     8	\label{sec:strat}
     9	
    10	\begin{definition}[Two-player one-round games]
    11	  \label{def:game}
    12	  A \emph{two-player one-round game} $\game$ is specified by a tuple
    13	  $(\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ where
    14	  \begin{enumerate}
    15	  \item $\cal{X}$ and $\cal{Y}$ are finite sets (called the \emph{question
    16	      alphabets}),
    17	  \item $\cal{A}$ and $\cal{B}$ are finite sets (called the \emph{answer
    18	      alphabets}),
    19	  \item $\mu$ is a probability distribution over $\cal{X} \times \cal{Y}$
    20	    (called the \emph{question distribution}), and
    21	  \item $D: \cal{X} \times \cal{Y} \times \cal{A} \times \cal{B} \to \{0,1\}$ is
    22	    a function (called the \emph{decision predicate}).
    23	  \end{enumerate}
    24	\end{definition}
    25	
    26	\begin{definition}[Tensor product strategies]
    27	  \label{def:tensor-product-strategy}
    28	  A \emph{tensor product strategy} $\strategy$ for a game $\game = (\cal{X},
    29	  \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is a tuple $(\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ where
    30	  \begin{itemize}
    31		\item $\ket{\psi}$ is a pure quantum state, i.e.\ a unit vector in $\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ for finite
    32	    dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $\mH_A, \mH_B$,
    33		\item $A$ is a set $\{A^x\}$ such that for every $x \in \cal{X}$, $A^x =
    34	    \{A^x_a \}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is a POVM over $\mH_A$, and
    35		\item $B$ is a set $\{B^y\}$ such that for every $y \in \cal{Y}$, $B^y =
    36	    \{B^y_b \}_{b \in \cal{B}}$ is a POVM over $\mH_B$.
    37	\end{itemize}
    38	\end{definition}
    39	
    40	\begin{definition}[Tensor product value]
    41	  \label{def:tensor-product-value}
    42		The \emph{tensor product value} of a tensor product strategy $\strategy =
    43	  (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$  with respect to a game $\game=(\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A},
    44	  \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is defined as
    45	  \begin{equation*}
    46			\val^*(\game, \strategy) = \sum_{x,\, y,\, a,\, b} \, \mu(x,y)\, D(x,y,a,b)\,
    47	    \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^y_b\, \ket{\psi}\;.
    48	  \end{equation*}
    49		For $v\in[0,1]$ we say that the strategy $\strategy$ \emph{passes (or wins)
    50	    $\game$ with probability $v$ if} $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \geq v$.
    51	  The \emph{tensor product value} of $\game$ is defined as
    52	  \begin{equation*}
    53			\val^*(\game) = \sup_\strategy \val^*(\game, \strategy)\;,
    54	  \end{equation*}
    55		where the supremum is taken over all tensor product strategies $\strategy$ for
    56	  $\game$.
    57	\end{definition}
    58	
    59	
    60	\begin{remark}
    61	  Unless specified otherwise, all strategies considered in this paper are tensor
    62	  product strategies, and we simply call them \emph{strategies}.
    63	  Similarly, we refer to $\val^*(\game)$ as the \emph{value} of the game
    64	  $\game$.
    65	\end{remark}
    66	
    67	
    68	\begin{definition}[Projective strategies]
    69	  \label{def:projective-strategy}
    70	  We say that a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ is \emph{projective} if
    71	  all the measurements $\{A^x_a\}_a$ and $\{B^y_b\}_b$ are projective.
    72	\end{definition}
    73	
    74	\begin{definition}\label{rem:symmetric-games}
    75		A game $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is
    76	  \emph{symmetric} if the question and answer alphabets are the same for both
    77	  players (i.e.\
    78	  $\cal{X} = \cal{Y}$ and $\cal{A} = \cal{B}$), the distribution $\mu$ is
    79	  symmetric (i.e.\
    80	  $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y,x)$), and the decision predicate $D$ treats both players
    81	  symmetrically (i.e.\ for all $x,y,a,b$, $D(x,y,a,b) = D(y,x,b,a)$).
    82	 
    83	We call a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$
    84	  \emph{symmetric} if $\ket{\psi}$ is a (pure) state in $\mH \otimes \mH$, for some
    85	  Hilbert space $\mH$, that is invariant under permutation of the two factors,
    86	  and the measurement operators of both players are identical.
    87	\end{definition}
    88	
    89	We often specify symmetric games $\game$ and symmetric strategies $\strategy$ using
    90	  a compact notation: we write $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A}, \mu, D)$ and
   205	  the players never return different answers when simultaneously asked the same
   206	  question.
   207	  As shown in~\cite{paulsen2016estimating} the condition for a
   208	  finite-dimensional strategy of being synchronous is equivalent to the
   209	  condition that it is projective, consistent, and moreover $\ket{\psi}$ is a
   210	  maximally entangled state.
   211	  (The equivalence is extended to infinite-dimensional strategies, as well as
   212	  correlations induced by limits of finite-dimensional strategies,
   213	  in~\cite{kim2018synchronous}.)
   214	\end{remark}

     5	/-!
     6	# Subspaces for the Pauli basis test
     7	
     8	This module supplies the register subspaces, dot-product orthogonals, and the
     9	canonical coordinate complement used by the conditionally linear maps.  The
    10	canonical complement is presented through the intrinsic pivot-rank test; the
    11	equivalence with a particular row-reduced-echelon implementation is a later
    12	construction theorem.
    13	
    14	## References
    15	
    16	The statement-level definitions are `def:register-subspace`,
    17	`def:dot-product-orthogonal`, `def:canonical-complement`, and
    18	`def:cl-canonical` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex`;
    19	the paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-384`.
    20	-/
    21	
    22	open scoped BigOperators
    23	
    24	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    25	
    26	variable {K ι : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    27	
    28	/--
    29	`registerSubmodule K S` is the span of the standard coordinate vectors indexed
    30	by `S`.  It is the Lean encoding of `def:register-subspace` from
    31	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:24-29`, whose paper origin is
    32	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-239`.
    33	-/
    34	def registerSubmodule (K : Type*) [Field K] (S : Finset ι) : Submodule K (ι → K) :=
    35	  Submodule.span K {v | ∃ i, i ∈ S ∧ v = Pi.single i 1}
    36	
    37	/--
    38	`dotOrthogonal W` consists of vectors whose coordinate dot product with every
    39	member of `W` vanishes.  This is `def:dot-product-orthogonal` in
    40	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:31-42`, with paper origin
    41	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:241-255`.
    42	-/
    43	def dotOrthogonal (W : Submodule K (ι → K)) : Submodule K (ι → K) where
    44	  carrier := {u | ∀ v, v ∈ W → dotProduct u v = 0}
    45	  zero_mem' := by
    46	    intro v hv
    47	    simp [dotProduct]
    48	  add_mem' := by
    49	    intro u v hu hv w hw
    50	    calc
    51	      dotProduct (u + v) w =
    52	          (dotProduct u w) + (dotProduct v w) := by
    53	            change (∑ i, (u i + v i) * w i) =
    54	              (∑ i, u i * w i) + (∑ i, v i * w i)
    55	            simp_rw [add_mul]
    56	            rw [Finset.sum_add_distrib]
    57	      _ = 0 := by rw [hu w hw, hv w hw, add_zero]
    58	  smul_mem' := by
    59	    intro c u hu v hv
    60	    calc
    61	      dotProduct (c • u) v = c * dotProduct u v := by
    62	        simp [dotProduct, smul_eq_mul, mul_assoc, Finset.mul_sum]
    63	      _ = 0 := by rw [hu v hv, mul_zero]
    64	
    65	/-- Restrict a coordinate vector to the first `k` coordinates.  Lean-only rank
    66	infrastructure for `def:canonical-complement`, blueprint
    67	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:84-110`, paper `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-384`.
    68	-/
    69	private def prefixMap (k n : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) :
    70	    (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] (Fin k → K) :=
    71	  { toFun := fun x i => x ⟨i.1, lt_of_lt_of_le i.2 hk⟩
    72	    map_add' := by
    73	      intro x y
    74	      rfl
    75	    map_smul' := by
    76	      intro c x
    77	      rfl }
    78	
    79	/-- The rank of a prefix restriction used by the pivot characterization. -/
    80	private noncomputable def prefixRank {n : ℕ} (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K))
    81	    (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) : ℕ :=
    82	  Module.finrank K (W.map (prefixMap k n hk))
    83	
    84	/--
    85	The non-pivot coordinate set of `W`, defined by the rank-increase
    86	characterization of pivots.  This is the basis-free encoding approved for
    87	`def:canonical-complement` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:84-110`;
    88	the paper's Gaussian-elimination presentation is
    89	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:303-320`.
    90	-/
    91	noncomputable def canonicalComplement {n : ℕ}
    92	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) : Finset (Fin n) :=
    93	  Finset.univ.filter fun j =>
    94	    prefixRank W (j.1 + 1) (Nat.succ_le_of_lt j.2) =
    95	      prefixRank W j.1 j.2.le
    96	
    97	/--
    98	The canonical coordinate complement spans a complement of `W`.  This is the
    99	proposition `lem:canonical-complement` in
   100	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:112-120`, with paper origin
   101	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:342-373`.
   102	The proof is intentionally deferred in the stage-4.1 skeleton.
   103	-/
   104	theorem isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement {n : ℕ}
   105	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) :
   106	    IsCompl W (registerSubmodule K (canonicalComplement W)) := by
   107	  sorry
   108	
   109	/--
   110	The projector onto the canonical coordinate complement along `W`.  This is
   111	`def:cl-canonical` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:133-145`,
   112	originating at `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:375-384`.
   113	-/
   114	noncomputable def canonicalProjOfKernel {n : ℕ}
   115	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) : (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] (Fin n → K) := by
   116	  let T := registerSubmodule K (canonicalComplement W)
   117	  let p : (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] T :=
   118	    Submodule.projectionOnto T W
   119	      (isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement W).symm
   120	  exact T.subtype.comp p
   121
