   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed

900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}

  1073	\paragraph{Conditional linear functions for the Pauli basis test.}
  1074	The CL functions corresponding to the Pauli basis test question distribution are
  1075	parameterized by the parameter tuple $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$.
  1076	Let $V^\pauli$ denote the linear space $(\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m
  1077	\times (\F_q)^2$.
  1078	The space $V^\pauli$ is decomposed into a direct sum of the following register
  1079	subspaces: $V_\xpt,V_\zpt$ (which are $m$-dimensional), $V_\coord$ (which is
  1080	$1$-dimensional), $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is $m$-dimensional), and
  1081	$V_{\rxpt},V_{\rzpt}$ (which are $1$-dimensional).
  1082	We identify elements of $V^\pauli$ as tuples $(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1083	\in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m \times (\F_q)^2$.
  1084	We define CL functions $L_\tvar: V^\pauli \to V^\pauli$ for every type $\tvar
  1085	\in \type^\pauli$:
  1086	\begin{enumerate}
  1087	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Point,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1088	  = L_\Point(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\Point$ is the $1$-level CL function defined in
  1089	  \Cref{eq:cl-ptf}.\footnote{The range $V_{\xpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus
  1090	    V_{\dir{}}$ or $V_{\zpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ of $L_\Point$ is
  1091	    embedded in $V^\pauli$ in the natural way.
  1092	    The same convention is used also in Item 2 and 3 for $L_\ALine$ and
  1093	    $L_\DLine$.}
  1094	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\ALine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1095	  = L_\ALine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\ALine$ is the $2$-level CL function defined in
  1096	  \Cref{eq:cl-alnf}.
  1097	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\DLine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1098	  = L_\DLine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\DLine$ is the $3$-level CL function defined in
  1099	  \Cref{eq:cl-dlnf}.
  1100	\item For $\tvar \in \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair, (\Pair,X), (\Pair,Z) \}$,
  1101	  $L_{\tvar}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) =
  1102	  (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,0,0,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$, i.e., it projects onto $V_\xpt \oplus
  1103	  V_\zpt \oplus V_{\rxpt} \oplus V_{\rzpt}$.
  1104	  Thus $L_{\tvar}$ is a $1$-level CL function.
  1105

  1107	  function.

  1426	\paragraph{Soundness of the Pauli basis test.} 
  1427	We state the soundness properties of the Pauli basis test.
  1428	The following is an adaptation of the self-testing statement in~\cite[Theorem
  1429	6.4]{NW19}.
  1430	
  1431	\begin{theorem}
  1432	  \label{thm:pauli}
  1433	There exists a function 
  1434	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1435	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1436	\begin{enumerate}
  1437	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1438	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1439	    \begin{gather*}
  1440	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1441	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
  1442	    \end{gather*}
  1443	    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$.

65	\begin{definition}[Graph distribution]
    66	  \label{def:graph-distribution}
    67	  Let $G = (U, E)$ be an undirected graph with vertex set $U$ and edge set~$E$.
    68	  Edges in~$E$ are written as multisets $\{u, v\}$ of two vertices; the case $u
    69	  = v$ represents a self-loop.
    70	  Suppose there are $m$ edges, $k$ of which are self-loops.
    71	  Then the \emph{graph distribution $\mu_G$ of~$G$} is the distribution over
    72	  $U\times U$ such that for every $(u, v)\in U\times U$,
    73	  \begin{equation*}
    74	    \mu_G(u, v) =
    75	    \begin{cases}
    76	      1/(2m-k) & \text{if $\{u, v\} \in E$},\\
    77	      0 & \text{otherwise}.
    78	    \end{cases}
    79	  \end{equation*}
    80	  This is identical to the uniform distribution over pairs $(u, v)\in U\times U$
    81	  such that $\{u, v\} \in E$.
    82	\end{definition}

    10	\begin{definition}[Two-player one-round games]
    11	  \label{def:game}
    12	  A \emph{two-player one-round game} $\game$ is specified by a tuple
    13	  $(\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ where
    14	  \begin{enumerate}
    15	  \item $\cal{X}$ and $\cal{Y}$ are finite sets (called the \emph{question
    16	      alphabets}),
    17	  \item $\cal{A}$ and $\cal{B}$ are finite sets (called the \emph{answer
    18	      alphabets}),
    19	  \item $\mu$ is a probability distribution over $\cal{X} \times \cal{Y}$
    20	    (called the \emph{question distribution}), and
    21	  \item $D: \cal{X} \times \cal{Y} \times \cal{A} \times \cal{B} \to \{0,1\}$ is
    22	    a function (called the \emph{decision predicate}).
    23	  \end{enumerate}
    24	\end{definition}
    25	
    26	\begin{definition}[Tensor product strategies]
    27	  \label{def:tensor-product-strategy}
    28	  A \emph{tensor product strategy} $\strategy$ for a game $\game = (\cal{X},
    29	  \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is a tuple $(\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ where
    30	  \begin{itemize}
    31		\item $\ket{\psi}$ is a pure quantum state, i.e.\ a unit vector in $\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ for finite
    32	    dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $\mH_A, \mH_B$,
    33		\item $A$ is a set $\{A^x\}$ such that for every $x \in \cal{X}$, $A^x =
    34	    \{A^x_a \}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is a POVM over $\mH_A$, and
    35		\item $B$ is a set $\{B^y\}$ such that for every $y \in \cal{Y}$, $B^y =
    36	    \{B^y_b \}_{b \in \cal{B}}$ is a POVM over $\mH_B$.
    37	\end{itemize}
    38	\end{definition}
    39	
    40	\begin{definition}[Tensor product value]
    41	  \label{def:tensor-product-value}
    42		The \emph{tensor product value} of a tensor product strategy $\strategy =
    43	  (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$  with respect to a game $\game=(\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A},
    44	  \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is defined as
    45	  \begin{equation*}
    46			\val^*(\game, \strategy) = \sum_{x,\, y,\, a,\, b} \, \mu(x,y)\, D(x,y,a,b)\,
    47	    \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^y_b\, \ket{\psi}\;.
    48	  \end{equation*}
    49		For $v\in[0,1]$ we say that the strategy $\strategy$ \emph{passes (or wins)
    50	    $\game$ with probability $v$ if} $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \geq v$.
    51	  The \emph{tensor product value} of $\game$ is defined as
    52	  \begin{equation*}
    53			\val^*(\game) = \sup_\strategy \val^*(\game, \strategy)\;,
    54	  \end{equation*}
    55		where the supremum is taken over all tensor product strategies $\strategy$ for
    56	  $\game$.
    57	\end{definition}
    58	
    59	
    60	\begin{remark}
    61	  Unless specified otherwise, all strategies considered in this paper are tensor
    62	  product strategies, and we simply call them \emph{strategies}.
    63	  Similarly, we refer to $\val^*(\game)$ as the \emph{value} of the game
    64	  $\game$.
    65	\end{remark}
    66	
    67	
    68	\begin{definition}[Projective strategies]
    69	  \label{def:projective-strategy}
    70	  We say that a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ is \emph{projective} if
    71	  all the measurements $\{A^x_a\}_a$ and $\{B^y_b\}_b$ are projective.
    72	\end{definition}
    73	
    74	\begin{definition}\label{rem:symmetric-games}
    75		A game $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is
    76	  \emph{symmetric} if the question and answer alphabets are the same for both
    77	  players (i.e.\
    78	  $\cal{X} = \cal{Y}$ and $\cal{A} = \cal{B}$), the distribution $\mu$ is
    79	  symmetric (i.e.\
    80	  $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y,x)$), and the decision predicate $D$ treats both players
    81	  symmetrically (i.e.\ for all $x,y,a,b$, $D(x,y,a,b) = D(y,x,b,a)$).
    82	 
    83	We call a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$

    85	  Hilbert space $\mH$, that is invariant under permutation of the two factors,

   216	
   217	We introduce several distance measures that are used throughout.
   218	
   219	\begin{definition}[Distance between states]
   220	  \label{def:state-distance}
   221	
   222		Let $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}_{n\in \N}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}_{n\in \N}$ be two
   223	  families of states in the same space $\mH$.
   224	  For some function $\delta : \N \to [0,1]$ we say that $\{ \ket{\psi_n} \}$ and
   225	  $\{ \ket{\psi'_n} \}$ are \emph{$\delta$-close}, denoted as $\ket{\psi}
   226	  \approx_\delta \ket{\psi'}$, if $ \norm{\ket{\psi_n} - \ket{\psi'_n}}^2 =
   227	  O(\delta(n))$.
   228	  (For convenience we generally leave the dependence of the states and $\delta$
   229	  on the indexing parameter $n$ implicit, writing e.g.\ $\ket{\psi}$ for $\ket{\psi_n}$.)
   230	\end{definition}
   231	
   232	\begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]
   233	  \label{def:consistency}
   234		Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$.
   235	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}_A \otimes \cal{H}_B$ be a quantum state, and for
   236	  all $x\in \mX$, $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ POVMs.
   237	  We write
   238	  \begin{equation*}
   239	    A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \simeq_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a
   240	  \end{equation*}
   241	  on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
   242	  \begin{equation*}
   243	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_{a\ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^x_b \ket{\psi}
   244	    = O(\delta)\;.\footnote{Here the use of the $O(\cdot)$ notation refers to the fact that the notation will often be used to measure consistency for \emph{famillies} of POVM and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n\in \mathbb{N}$, which will always be clear from context but omitted for legibility, see Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}. The $O(\cdot)$ is taken as $n\to\infty$.}
   245	  \end{equation*}
   246	  In this case, we say that $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are
   247	  \emph{$\delta$-consistent} on $\ket{\psi}$.
   248	\end{definition}
   249	
   250	Note that a consistent measurement on $\ket{\psi}$ according to
   251	Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement} is $0$-consistent with itself on the same $\ket{\psi}$ and under
   252	the singleton distribution, according to Definition~\ref{def:consistency} (and
   253	vice-versa). This is because 
   254	\[ \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi} =1 \,\implies \, \forall a\;,\;\Id\otimes M_a \ket{\psi} = M_a \otimes \Id \ket{\psi}\;,\]
   255	because using that $\{M_a\}$ is a POVM there must be equality in the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
   256	\[ 1 = \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\, \leq\, \Big(\sum_a \|\Id\otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\|^2 \Big)\Big(\sum_a \|M_a\otimes \Id \ket{\psi}\|^2 \Big)^{1/2} \,\leq\,1 \;.\]
   257	
   258	\begin{definition}[Distance between POVMs]
   259	  \label{def:povm-distance}
   260		Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$. 
   261	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}$ be a quantum state, and for all $x\in \mX$,
   262	  $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ two POVMs on $\mH$.
   263	  We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state
   264	    $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
   265	  \begin{equation*}
   266	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_a \norm{ (M^x_a - N^x_a) \ket{\psi} }^2 \leq O(\delta)\;,
   267	  \end{equation*}
   268	  and we write $M^x_a \approx_\delta N^x_a$ to denote this when the state
   269	  $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ are clear from context.
   270	  This distance is referred to as the \emph{state-dependent} distance.
   271	\end{definition}

    63	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a := rfl
    64	
    65	/-- Push-forward preserves total mass. -/
    66	theorem map_totalWeight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    67	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    68	    (𝒟.map e).totalWeight = 𝒟.totalWeight := by
    69	  simpa [totalWeight, map] using
    70	    (Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    71	      (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    72	      (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩) 𝒟.weight)
    73	
    74	/-- A finite weighted sum over a push-forward distribution is the corresponding
    75	weighted sum of the pulled-back family.  This is the `Distribution` analogue of
    76	the finite-sum form of `PMF.map`. -/
    77	theorem map_sum_smul {α β M : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    78	    [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
    79	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (f : β → M) :
    80	    ∑ b ∈ (𝒟.map e).support, (𝒟.map e).weight b • f b =
    81	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    82	  classical
    83	  calc
    84	    ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    85	        (∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a) • f b
    86	        = ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    87	            ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    88	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    89	          intro b _
    90	          rw [Finset.sum_smul]
    91	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    92	          intro a ha
    93	          exact congrArg (fun x => 𝒟.weight a • f x) (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2.symm
    94	    _ = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    95	          exact Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    96	            (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    97	            (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩)
    98	            (fun a => 𝒟.weight a • f (e a))
    99	
   100	end Distribution
   101	
   102	/-- On a finite ambient type, a summand that vanishes outside a distribution's
   103	explicit support has the same total sum over all ambient values as over that support.
   104	
   105	This is a project-local explicit-support adapter around Mathlib's `Finset.sum_subset`:
   106	Mathlib supplies the finite-sum theorem, while this lemma packages the common shape used
   107	when paper expressions sum over a whole question set but the repository stores a smaller
   108	`Distribution.support`.  It is not intended to replace Mathlib probability theory. -/
   109	theorem Distribution.sum_univ_eq_sum_support {α β : Type*} [Fintype α]
   110	    [AddCommMonoid β] (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → β)
   111	    (hf : ∀ a, a ∉ 𝒟.support → f a = 0) :
   112	    (∑ a : α, f a) = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, f a := by
   113	  classical
   114	  simpa using
   115	    (Finset.sum_subset (Finset.subset_univ 𝒟.support)
   116	      (fun a _ ha => hf a ha)).symm
   117	
   118	namespace Distribution.IsProbability
   119	
   120	/-- Unpack the equality form of the probability invariant. -/
   121	theorem weight_sum_eq_one {α : Type*}
   122	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   123	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a = 1 := by
   124	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.totalWeight] using h𝒟
   125	
   126	/-- On a finite ambient type, a probabilistic `Distribution` has total weight `1` even
   127	when its weights are summed over the whole ambient type.
   128	
   129	This packages the explicit-support bookkeeping in `Distribution` for downstream Lean
   130	statements that follow the paper's notation `𝔼_{x ∼ 𝒟}` over the question set rather
   131	than over a stored support finset. -/
   132	theorem weight_sum_univ_eq_one {α : Type*} [Fintype α]
   133	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   134	    (∑ a : α, 𝒟.weight a) = 1 := by
   135	  rw [Distribution.sum_univ_eq_sum_support 𝒟 𝒟.weight 𝒟.outsideSupport]
   136	  exact h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one
   137	
   138	/-- A probability distribution has total weight at most `1`. -/
   139	theorem weight_sum_le_one {α : Type*}
   140	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   141	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a ≤ 1 :=
   142	  le_of_eq h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one
   143	
   144	/-- Push-forward preserves the probability invariant. -/
   145	theorem map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
   146	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (e : α → β) :
   147	    (𝒟.map e).IsProbability := by
   148	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.map_totalWeight] using h𝒟
   149	
   150	end Distribution.IsProbability

   153	
   154	/-- The Mathlib probability mass function associated to a project `Distribution`
   155	whose total mass is one.

   157	The construction sends each nonnegative real weight to `ℝ≥0∞` by

   164	      rw [← ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg (fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a),
   165	        h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one]
   166	      simp)
   167	    (by
   168	      intro a ha
   169	      rw [𝒟.outsideSupport a ha]
   170	      simp)

   172	@[simp]
   173	theorem toPMF_apply {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   174	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (a : α) :
   175	    𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a = ENNReal.ofReal (𝒟.weight a) := rfl
   176

   178	theorem toPMF_apply_toReal {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   179	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (a : α) :
   180	    (𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a).toReal = 𝒟.weight a := by

     3	/-!
     4	# Uniform subset estimates
     5	
     6	This file contains estimates for the total variation distance between the
     7	uniform distribution on a finite type and the uniform distribution on a
     8	nonempty finite subset, together with averaging bounds for `[0,1]`-valued
     9	functions.  The uniform-subset total-variation identity is proved by transport
    10	through Mathlib probability mass functions.
    11	-/
    12	
    13	open scoped BigOperators
    14	
    15	namespace MIPStarRE.LDT
    16	
    17	/-- Total variation between the uniform distribution on a finite ambient type and
    18	the uniform distribution on a nonempty finite subset.
    19	
    20	This is the elementary finite identity
    21	`TV(uniform α, uniform s) = 1 - |s| / |α|`.  The proof transports the project
    22	`Distribution` statement to Mathlib's uniform probability mass functions. -/
    23	theorem totalVariationDistance_uniformDistribution_uniformOnFinset_eq
    24	    {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α]
    25	    (s : Finset α) (hs : s.Nonempty) :
    26	    totalVariationDistance (uniformDistribution α) (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s) =
    27	      1 - (s.card : Error) / (Fintype.card α : Error) := by
    28	  rw [totalVariationDistance_eq_toPMF_sum]
    29	  change PMF.totalVariationDistance
    30	      ((uniformDistribution α).toPMF (uniformDistribution_isProbability α))
    31	      ((Distribution.uniformOnFinset s).toPMF
    32	        (Distribution.uniformOnFinset_isProbability s hs)) =
    33	    1 - (s.card : Error) / (Fintype.card α : Error)
    34	  rw [uniformDistribution_toPMF, Distribution.uniformOnFinset_toPMF]
    35	  exact PMF.totalVariationDistance_uniformOfFintype_uniformOfFinset_eq s hs
    36	
    37	/-- A `[0,1]`-valued function averaged over a nonempty finite subset is bounded
    38	by its ambient uniform average plus the total variation distance between the
    39	two uniform distributions. -/
    40	theorem avgOver_uniformOnFinset_le_uniformDistribution_add_totalVariationDistance
    41	    {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α]
    42	    (s : Finset α) (hs : s.Nonempty)
    43	    (f : α → Error)
    44	    (hf_nonneg : ∀ a, 0 ≤ f a)
    45	    (hf_le_one : ∀ a, f a ≤ 1) :
    46	    avgOver (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s) f
    47	      ≤ avgOver (uniformDistribution α) f
    48	        + totalVariationDistance (uniformDistribution α) (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s) := by
    49	  exact
    50	    avgOver_le_avgOver_add_totalVariationDistance
    51	      (uniformDistribution α) (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s)
    52	      (uniformDistribution_isProbability α)
    53	      (Distribution.uniformOnFinset_isProbability s hs)
    54	      f hf_nonneg hf_le_one
    55	
    56	end MIPStarRE.LDT

     3	/-!
     4	# Matrix-valued measurements for the MIP*=RE project
     5	
     6	This file provides the matrix-valued measurement layer used by the LDT formalization.
     7	
     8	## Main definitions
     9	
    10	* `Submeasurement` — a family of PSD matrices summing to at most the identity.
    11	* `Measurement` — a family of PSD matrices summing to exactly the identity.
    12	* `Submeasurement.postprocess` — data-processed submeasurements via answer relabeling.
    13	* `Measurement.postprocess` — the paper's postprocessing proposition for complete POVMs.
    14	* `inconsistency` — the off-diagonal mass `∑_{a ≠ b} τ(M_a N_b)`.
    15	* `diagOverlap` — the diagonal mass `∑_a τ(M_a N_a)`.
    16	
    17	## References
    18	
    19	This file builds the project's finite-dimensional measurement layer on top of
    20	the normalized-trace and positive-operator facts in `MIPStarRE.Quantum.FiniteMatrix`
    21	for the quantum formalization in `references/ldt-paper/`.
    22	-/
    23	
    24	open scoped BigOperators MatrixOrder Matrix ComplexOrder
    25	
    26	namespace MIPStarRE.Quantum
    27	
    28	/-! ## Submeasurements and measurements -/
    29	
    30	/--
    31	A submeasurement on a finite answer type `α` is a family of PSD matrices
    32	`M : α → Op d` with `∑ a, M a ≤ 1`.
    33	-/
    34	structure Submeasurement (α : Type*) [Fintype α] (d : Type*) [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d] where
    35	  /-- The effect operators. -/
    36	  effect : α → Op d
    37	  /-- Each effect is positive semidefinite. -/
    38	  pos : ∀ a, 0 ≤ effect a
    39	  /-- The effects sum to at most the identity. -/
    40	  sum_le_one : ∑ a, effect a ≤ 1
    41	
    42	/--
    43	A measurement is a submeasurement whose effects sum exactly to the identity.
    44	-/
    45	structure Measurement (α : Type*) [Fintype α] (d : Type*) [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    46	    extends Submeasurement α d where
    47	  /-- The effects sum to the identity. -/
    48	  sum_eq_one : ∑ a, effect a = 1
    49	
    50	/-! ## Totals and postprocessing -/
    51	
    52	namespace Submeasurement
    53	
    54	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    55	variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
    56	
    57	/-! ### Totals and postprocessing -/
    58	
    59	/-- The total operator `∑ a, M_a`. -/
    60	noncomputable def total (M : Submeasurement α d) : Op d :=
    61	  ∑ a, M.effect a
    62	
    63	/--
    64	Data processing: relabel the answer set by `f : α → β`, summing the effects over
    65	fibers.
    66	-/
    67	noncomputable def postprocess [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    68	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) : Submeasurement β d where
    69	  effect b := ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
    70	  pos b := Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => M.pos a
    71	  sum_le_one := by
    72	    calc
    73	      ∑ b, ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
    74	          = ∑ a, M.effect a := Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect
    75	      _ ≤ 1 := M.sum_le_one
    76	
    77	/-- Restatement of `sum_le_one` in terms of the named total operator. -/
    78	theorem total_le_one (M : Submeasurement α d) :
    79	    M.total ≤ 1 := by
    80	  simpa [total] using M.sum_le_one
    81	
    82	/-- Postprocessing preserves the sum of all effects. -/
    83	theorem postprocess_sum_eq [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    84	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) :
    85	    ∑ a, M.effect a = ∑ b, (M.postprocess f).effect b :=
    86	  (Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect).symm
    87	
    88	/-- Postprocessing preserves the named total operator. -/
    89	theorem postprocess_total [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    90	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) :
    91	    (M.postprocess f).total = M.total := by
    92	  simpa [total] using (M.postprocess_sum_eq f).symm
    93	
    94	end Submeasurement
    95	
    96	namespace Measurement
    97	
    98	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    99	variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
   100	
   101	/--
   102	Build a complete measurement from effects whose sum is exactly the identity.
   103	
   104	This constructor keeps the equality proof as the primary hypothesis and derives
   105	the inherited submeasurement inequality automatically.  It is useful at paper
   106	sites that are explicitly POVMs rather than relaxed sub-POVMs.
   107	-/
   108	def ofSumEqOne (effect : α → Op d) (pos : ∀ a, 0 ≤ effect a)
   109	    (sum_eq_one : ∑ a, effect a = 1) : Measurement α d where
   110	  effect := effect
   111	  pos := pos
   112	  sum_le_one := le_of_eq sum_eq_one
   113	  sum_eq_one := sum_eq_one
   114	
   115	/-- The named total of a complete measurement is the identity. -/
   116	theorem total_eq_one (M : Measurement α d) :
   117	    M.total = 1 :=
   118	  M.sum_eq_one
   119	
   120	/--
   121	Postprocess a complete measurement by relabeling outcomes.
   122	
   123	This formalizes `references/ldt-paper/preliminaries.tex:169--180`: regrouping
   124	the effects along the fibers of `f` preserves the total operator, so a POVM
   125	remains a POVM after postprocessing.
   126	-/
   127	noncomputable def postprocess [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   128	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) : Measurement β d where
   129	  toSubmeasurement := M.toSubmeasurement.postprocess f
   130	  sum_eq_one := by
   131	    calc
   132	      ∑ b, ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
   133	          = ∑ a, M.effect a := Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect
   134	      _ = 1 := M.sum_eq_one
   135	
   136	@[simp] theorem postprocess_effect [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   137	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) (b : β) :
   138	    (M.postprocess f).effect b =
   139	      ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a :=
   140	  rfl
   141	
   142	@[simp] theorem postprocess_to_submeasurement [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   143	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) :
   144	    (M.postprocess f).toSubmeasurement = M.toSubmeasurement.postprocess f :=
   145	  rfl
   146	
   147	end Measurement
   148	
   149	/-! ## Overlap definitions -/
   150	
   151	section Overlap
   152	
   153	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
   154	variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
   155	
   156	/-- The off-diagonal overlap mass `∑_{a ≠ b} τ(M_a N_b)`. -/
   157	noncomputable def inconsistency (M N : α → Op d) : ℂ :=
   158	  ∑ a, ∑ b ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun b => b ≠ a), normalizedTrace (M a * N b)
   159	
   160	/-- The diagonal overlap mass `∑_a τ(M_a N_a)`. -/
   161	noncomputable def diagOverlap (M N : α → Op d) : ℂ :=
   162	  ∑ a, normalizedTrace (M a * N a)
   163	
   164	end Overlap
   165	
   166	end MIPStarRE.Quantum

     3	/-!

     5	
     6	This module contains the elementary trace and matrix-algebra facts used by the
     7	finite-dimensional quantum layer.  It introduces the local operator abbreviation
     8	`Op d = Matrix d d ℂ` and keeps the basic trace bookkeeping independent of the

    11	## References

    18	open WithLp

    20	namespace Matrix
    21	
    22	/-! ### Trace bookkeeping -/
    23	
    24	/-- Reindexing rows and columns by the same equivalence preserves matrix trace.
    25	
    26	This generic matrix lemma is used when moving between equivalent finite index
    27	presentations of the same operator. -/
    28	theorem trace_reindex {α β R : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
    29	    [AddCommMonoid R] (e : α ≃ β) (M : Matrix α α R) :
    30	    Matrix.trace (Matrix.reindex e e M) = Matrix.trace M := by
    31	  classical
    32	  simp only [Matrix.trace, Matrix.diag_apply, Matrix.reindex_apply]
    33	  rw [← e.symm.sum_comp (fun i : α => M i i)]
    34	  rfl
    35	
    36	/-! ### Linear matrix maps -/
    37	
    38	/-- Taking a submatrix is linear in the ambient matrix.
    39	
    40	This packages the entrywise linearity of `Matrix.submatrix` in the same style
    41	as Mathlib's block-diagonal additive and linear maps. -/
    42	def submatrixLinearMap (R : Type*) {m n m' n' α : Type*}
    43	    [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid α] [Module R α]
    44	    (row : m' → m) (col : n' → n) :
    45	    Matrix m n α →ₗ[R] Matrix m' n' α where
    46	  toFun := fun A => Matrix.submatrix A row col
    47	  map_add' := by
    48	    intro A B
    49	    ext i j
    50	    rfl
    51	  map_smul' := by
    52	    intro c A
    53	    ext i j
    54	    rfl
    55	
    56	@[simp]
    57	theorem submatrixLinearMap_apply (R : Type*) {m n m' n' α : Type*}
    58	    [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid α] [Module R α]
    59	    (row : m' → m) (col : n' → n) (A : Matrix m n α) :
    60	    Matrix.submatrixLinearMap R row col A = Matrix.submatrix A row col :=
    61	  rfl
    62	
    63	/-- The trace pairing of two block-diagonal matrices is the sum of the trace
    64	pairings of the corresponding diagonal blocks. -/
    65	theorem trace_blockDiagonal_mul {o m R : Type*}
    66	    [Fintype o] [DecidableEq o] [Fintype m] [NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring R]
    67	    (B D : o → Matrix m m R) :
    68	    Matrix.trace (Matrix.blockDiagonal B * Matrix.blockDiagonal D) =
    69	      ∑ b : o, Matrix.trace (B b * D b) := by
    70	  rw [← Matrix.blockDiagonal_mul B D, Matrix.trace_blockDiagonal]
    71	
    72	end Matrix

    75	
    76	/-! ### Basic operator type -/
    77	
    78	/-- Square complex matrices as the finite-dimensional operator algebra. -/
    79	abbrev Op (d : Type*) := Matrix d d ℂ
    80	
    81	/-! ### Kronecker product bookkeeping -/
    82	
    83	/-- Kronecker product is additive in the right factor, rewritten for subtraction. -/
    84	theorem kronecker_sub_right
    85	    {d₁ d₂ : Type*} {A : Op d₁} {B₁ B₂ : Op d₂} :
    86	    Matrix.kronecker A B₁ - Matrix.kronecker A B₂ =
    87	      Matrix.kronecker A (B₁ - B₂) := by
    88	  have hneg : Matrix.kronecker A (-B₂) = -Matrix.kronecker A B₂ := by
    89	    simpa using (Matrix.kronecker_smul (-1 : ℂ) A B₂)
    90	  calc
    91	    Matrix.kronecker A B₁ - Matrix.kronecker A B₂
    92	        = Matrix.kronecker A B₁ + Matrix.kronecker A (-B₂) := by
    93	            rw [hneg]
    94	            simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
    95	    _ = Matrix.kronecker A (B₁ - B₂) := by
    96	          simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using (Matrix.kronecker_add A B₁ (-B₂)).symm
    97	
    98	/-- Kronecker product is additive in the left factor, rewritten for subtraction. -/
    99	theorem kronecker_sub_left
   100	    {d₁ d₂ : Type*} {A₁ A₂ : Op d₁} {B : Op d₂} :
   101	    Matrix.kronecker A₁ B - Matrix.kronecker A₂ B =
   102	      Matrix.kronecker (A₁ - A₂) B := by
   103	  have hneg : Matrix.kronecker (-A₂) B = -Matrix.kronecker A₂ B := by
   104	    simpa using (Matrix.smul_kronecker (-1 : ℂ) A₂ B)
   105	  calc
   106	    Matrix.kronecker A₁ B - Matrix.kronecker A₂ B
   107	        = Matrix.kronecker A₁ B + Matrix.kronecker (-A₂) B := by
   108	            rw [hneg]
   109	            simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
   110	    _ = Matrix.kronecker (A₁ - A₂) B := by
   111	          simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using (Matrix.add_kronecker A₁ (-A₂) B).symm
   112	
   113	end MIPStarRE.Quantum

900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}
   916	
   917	Finally, for any $H \subseteq \F_q$ we define the \emph{decoding} map
   918	$\coded_H(\cdot)$ which takes as input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and
   919	returns the following vector $a \in \F_q^M$: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, if $g(y)
   920	\in H$, then set $a_y = g(y)$, and otherwise set $a_y = 0$.
   921	Note that for all $a \in H^M$ we have $\coded_H(g_a) = a$ where $g_a$ is the
   922	low-degree encoding of $a$.
   923	For notational brevity we often write $\coded(\cdot)$ to denote the boolean
   924	decoding map $\coded_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.

   926	\subsection{Linear spaces and registers}
   927	\label{sec:lin-reg}
   928	
   929	For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension $|V|$.
   930	The space $\C^V$ is endowed with a canonical orthonormal basis
   931	$\{\ket{x}\}_{x\in V}$.
   932	By ``a quantum state on $V$'' we mean a unit vector
   933	\begin{equation*}
   934	  \ket{\psi}_V \in \complex^V\;.
   935	\end{equation*}
   936	If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_k$ is the direct sum of subspaces $V_k$ over $\F$,
   937	then $\complex^V$ can be identified with $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k
   938	\complex^{V_i}$, by the identification of $\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus
   939	  x_k}$ with $\ket{x_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \ket{x_k}$.
   940	As a special case, if $\{e_i\}$ is a basis of $V$ the decomposition $V =
   941	\bigoplus_{i=1}^k ( \F e_i)$ yields the tensor product decomposition $\C^V =
   942	\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{\abs{\F}}$.
   943	We sometimes refer to the spaces $\C^{\abs{\F}}$ as the ``qudits'' of $\C^V$ (or
   944	of a state on it).
   945	
   946	\begin{definition}
   947	  \label{def:EPR}
   948	  For a linear space $V$ over a finite field $\F$, define the \EPR state on $\C^V
   949	  \otimes \C^V$ by
   950	  \begin{equation*}
   951	    \ket{\EPR}_V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\abs{V}}} \sum_{x\in V}\ket {x}\otimes \ket{x}\;.
   952	  \end{equation*}
   953	  We also write $\ket{\EPR}_{\F_q}$ as $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}$ as
   954	  $\ket{\EPR}$.
   955	\end{definition}
   956	
   957	\subsection{Measurements and observables}
   958	
   959	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued
   960	measures (POVMs).
   961	A POVM consists of a set of positive semidefinite operators $\{ M_a \}_{a\in S}$
   962	indexed by outcomes $a\in S$ that satisfy the condition $\sum_a M_a = I$. If the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \leq I$ then we refer to $\{M_a\}$ as a \emph{sub-measurement}.
   963	We sometimes use the same letter $M$ to refer to the collection of operators
   964	defining the POVM.
   965	The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on state $\ket{\psi}$
   966	is given by
   967	\begin{equation*}
   968	  \Pr(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\;.
   969	\end{equation*}
   970	A POVM $M=\{M_a\}$ is said to be \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a
   971	projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$). This automatically implies that operators
   972	$M_a, M_b$ for distinct outcomes $a \neq b$ are orthogonal ($M_a M_b =
   973	M_b M_a = 0$). An \emph{observable} is a unitary matrix.
   974	A \emph{binary observable} is an observable $O$ such that $O^2 = \Id$, i.e.\ $O$
   975	has eigenvalues in $\{-1,1\}$.
   976	
   977	We follow the convention that subscripts of the measurement index
   978	the outcome and superscripts of the measurement are used to index different
   979	measurements.
   980	For example, we use $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$ to represent a measurement indexed by $x$
   981	whose outcome consists of two parts $a$ and $b$.
   982	In this case, by slightly abusing the notation, we use $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$
   983	to denote
   984	\begin{equation*}
   985	  M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\, b}\;, \quad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\, b}\;.
   986	\end{equation*}
   987	For any $x$, $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$ are POVMs sometimes referred to as the
   988	``marginals'' of $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$.
   989	
   990	\begin{definition}
   991	  \label{def:bracket}
   992	  Let $\{M^x_a\}_{a\in A}$ be a family of POVMs indexed by $x\in \cal{X}$.
   993	  Let $f:A\to B$ be an arbitrary function.
   994	  We write $\bigl\{ M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} \bigr\}$ for the POVM derived from
   995	  $\{M^x_a\}$ by applying the function $f$ before returning the outcome.
   996	  More precisely,
   997	\begin{equation*}
   998	  M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]} = \sum_{a : f(a)=b} M^x_a\;.
   999	\end{equation*}
  1000	If $b$ is not in the image of $f$, then we define $M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]}$ to be
  1001	$0$. In cases where the outcome $a$ has a natural interpretation as a tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$ we sometimes slightly abuse notation and write $M^x_{[a_i=b]}$ for some $i\in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ to denote 
  1002	\[ M^x_{[a_i=b]} \,=\,\sum_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k):\,a_i=b} M^x_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k)}\;.\]
  1003	\end{definition}
  1004	
  1005	We will make frequent use of Naimark dilation. In our setting, it can be formulated as follows. For a proof, see~\cite[Theorem 5.1]{ML20}
  1006	
  1007	\begin{theorem}[Naimark dilation]\label{thm:naimark}

  1021	If we write $\ket{\widehat{\psi}} = \ket{\psi} \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}}$,

  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.

    50	finite cardinality ratio over `K^m`. -/
    51	noncomputable def polynomialAgreementProbability (m : ℕ) (K : Type*) [Field K] [Fintype K]
    52	    [DecidableEq K] (g h : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K) : ℚ≥0 :=
    53	  #{x ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin m → K)) |
    54	      MvPolynomial.eval x g = MvPolynomial.eval x h} /
    55	    (Fintype.card K ^ m : ℚ≥0)

    58	`p` is at most `m * d`. -/

    60	    {p : MvPolynomial (Fin m) K} (hdeg : ∀ i, p.degreeOf i ≤ d) :
    61	    p.totalDegree ≤ m * d := by
    62	  rw [MvPolynomial.totalDegree]
    63	  refine Finset.sup_le ?_
    64	  intro s hs
    65	  calc
    66	    s.sum (fun _ e => e) = ∑ i : Fin m, s i := by
    67	      rw [Finsupp.sum_fintype]
    68	      intro i
    69	      rfl
    70	    _ ≤ ∑ _i : Fin m, d := by
    71	      refine Finset.sum_le_sum ?_
    72	      intro i _
    73	      exact (MvPolynomial.degreeOf_le_iff.mp (hdeg i)) s hs

    81	    (hg : g.totalDegree ≤ d) (hh : h.totalDegree ≤ d) :
    82	    polynomialAgreementProbability m K g h ≤ d / Fintype.card K := by
    83	  have hsub_ne : g - h ≠ 0 := sub_ne_zero.mpr hneq
    84	  have hsub_deg : (g - h).totalDegree ≤ d :=
    85	    (MvPolynomial.totalDegree_sub g h).trans (max_le hg hh)
    86	  unfold polynomialAgreementProbability
    87	  rw [show {x ∈ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin m → K)) |
    88	        MvPolynomial.eval x g = MvPolynomial.eval x h} =

    97	      ≤ (g - h).totalDegree / Fintype.card K := by
    98	          simpa using
    99	            (MvPolynomial.schwartz_zippel_totalDegree
   100	              (n := m) (p := g - h) hsub_ne (Finset.univ : Finset K))

   106	theorem schwartzZippel_individualDegree {m d : ℕ} {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K]
   107	    [DecidableEq K] (g h : polyFunc m K d) (hneq : g ≠ h) :
   108	    polynomialAgreementProbability m K g.1 h.1 ≤ ((m * d : ℕ) : ℚ≥0) / Fintype.card K := by
   109	  have hval_ne : g.1 ≠ h.1 := by

   301		Let $q = 2^k$ be an admissible field size. For each odd $k$ we fix, once and

   304		$\{K_{e_i}\}_{i=1}^k$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis});

   306		representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is the $k$-bit string
   307		$\kappa(a) \in \F_2^k$, the \emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}; the two are
   308		freely identified. Addition of representations is bitwise addition modulo
   309		$2$, and multiplication is determined by the multiplication tables through
   310		\begin{equation}\label{eq:eq-mult}
   311			\kappa(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i\, \kappa(e_i b)
   312			= \sum_{i=1}^k a_i \bigl(K_{e_i}\, \kappa(b)\bigr)\;,
   313		\end{equation}
   314		where $\kappa(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$.

   318	% Paper label sec:ld-encoding kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   319	\label{sec:ld-encoding}

   321	\begin{definition}[Individual and total degree]\label{def:polynomials-degree}
   322		\uses{def:polyfunc}
   323		An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   324		\[
   325			f(x_1, \dots, x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m}
   326			c_\alpha\, x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   327		\]
   328		with coefficients $c_\alpha \in \F_q$; the coefficients are uniquely
   329		determined by $f$, since the $q^m$ monomial functions indexed by
   330		$\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m$ span the $q^m$-dimensional space of all
   331		functions $\F_q^m \to \F_q$ and are therefore linearly independent. The
   332		polynomial $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if
   333		$c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when $\alpha_i \le d$ for all $1 \le i \le m$, and
   334		\emph{total degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when
   335		$\sum_i \alpha_i \le d$. (Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are those
   336		of individual degree $1$.
   337		% Relationship to def:polyfunc: polyfunc keeps polynomial representatives,
   338		% so evaluation identifies it with the function classes above only for
   339		% d <= q-1.
   340		Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc} introduces the set $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ of
   341		polynomials in $\F_q[x_1, \dots, x_m]$ of degree at most $d$ in each
   342		variable, identified by their polynomial representatives rather than by the
   343		functions they induce. Evaluation maps $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ onto the set of
   344		$m$-variate polynomials of individual degree at most $\min(d, q-1)$ in the
   345		sense above; for $d \le q-1$ this map is a bijection, while for $d \ge q$
   346		distinct representatives, such as $x_1^q$ and $x_1$, induce the same
   347		function. Statements phrased in terms of $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ retain the
   348		representative convention of Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}.
   349	\end{definition}
   350	
   351	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz--Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]\label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   352		% Restatement of lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree under the source's label.
   353		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   354		Let $f, g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials of total degree at
   355		most $d$. Then
   356		\[
   357			\Prb_{\bx \sim \F_q^m}[f(\bx) = g(\bx)] \le \frac{d}{q}\;.
   358		\]
   359	\end{lemma}
   360	\begin{proof}
   361		\uses{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}
   362		This is Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}, stated and proved in
   363		Chapter~\ref{chap:preliminaries}; it is restated here under the label used
   364		by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   365	\end{proof}
   366	
   367	\begin{remark}\label{rem:schwartz-zippel-restated}
   368		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel} restates the total-degree bound of
   369		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree} under the label used by
   370		\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. The individual-degree consequence,
   371		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-individual}, shows that distinct elements of
   372		$\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ agree on at most an $md/q$ fraction of the points of
   373		$\F_q^m$; the analysis of the Pauli basis test uses the bound in this
   374		individual-degree form.
   375	\end{remark}
   376	
   377	The Schwartz--Zippel lemma implies that low-degree polynomials form an
   378	error-correcting code with good distance, the \emph{low-degree code} (a special
   379	case of the generalized Reed--Muller code).
   380	
   381	\begin{definition}[Low-degree encoding]\label{def:low-degree-encoding}
   382		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   383		Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$. For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$
   384		define the $m$-variate multilinear polynomial over $\F_q$
   385		\[
   386			\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)
   387			= \prod_{i : y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i : y_i = 0} (1 - x_i)\;,
   388		\]
   389		identifying $\{0,1\}$ with a subset of $\F_q$. Restricted to the subcube
   390		$\{0,1\}^m$, the polynomial $\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}$ vanishes everywhere except
   391		at $x = y$, where it equals $1$. For $a \in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates
   392		of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ (identifying $\{0,1\}^m$ with
   393		$\{1, \dots, M\}$ by the lexicographic ordering). The \emph{low-degree
   394		encoding of $a$} is the multilinear polynomial $g_a : \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   395		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   396		\begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   397			g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\;.
   398		\end{equation}
   399		For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ one has $g_a(y) = a_y$, and $g_a$ has total
   400		degree at most $m$.
   401	\end{definition}
   402	
   403	\begin{definition}[Indicator vector and linearity of the encoding]\label{def:indicator-vector}
   404		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   405		For $x \in \F_q^m$, the \emph{indicator vector} is
   406		\[
   407			\mathrm{ind}_m(x)
   408			= \bigl(\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\bigr)_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} \in \F_q^M\;.
   409		\]
   410		With this notation the low-degree encoding satisfies, for every
   411		$a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$,
   412		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   413		\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   414			g_a(x) = a \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(x)\;;
   415		\end{equation}
   416		in particular the map $a \mapsto g_a$ is $\F_q$-linear.
   417	\end{definition}
   418	
   419	Since encodings $g_a$ are multilinear, hence of total degree at most $m$, two
   420	encodings of distinct strings agree on at most an $m/q$ fraction of points of
   421	$\F_q^m$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel}.
   422	
   423	\begin{definition}[Decoding maps]\label{def:decoding-map}
   424		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding}
   425		For $H \subseteq \F_q$, the \emph{decoding map} $\mathrm{Dec}_H$ takes as
   426		input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and returns the vector
   427		$a \in \F_q^M$ defined by: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, set $a_y = g(y)$ if
   428		$g(y) \in H$, and $a_y = 0$ otherwise. For all $a \in H^M$ one has
   429		$\mathrm{Dec}_H(g_a) = a$. We write $\mathrm{Dec}(\cdot)$ for the boolean
   430		decoding map $\mathrm{Dec}_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.
   431	\end{definition}

   832	\subsection{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   833	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   834	
   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.
   849	For one, the classical and quantum low-degree tests of \Cref{sec:ldt} are
   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).
   855	
   856	We recall the Schwartz-Zippel lemma: 
   857	
   858	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz-Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]
   859	  \label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   860	  Let $f, g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials with total degree at most $d$. Then
   861	  \begin{equation*}
   862	    \Pr_{x \sim \F_q^m}[f(x) = g(x)] \leq d/q\;.
   863	  \end{equation*}
   864	\end{lemma}
   865	
   866	
   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).
   885	For any such $a$ define the multilinear polynomial $g_a: \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   886	called the \emph{low-degree encoding of $a$}, as follows:
   887	\begin{equation}
   888	\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   889		 g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)\;.
   890	\end{equation}
   891	Note that for any $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_a(y) = a_y$.
   892	Furthermore, the map $a\mapsto g_a$ is linear: for every $x \in \F_q^m$,
   893	\begin{equation}
   894	\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   895		g_a(x) = a \cdot \ind_m(x)\;,
   896	\end{equation}
   897	where $\ind_m(x)$ is the vector $(\ind_{m,y}(x))_{y \in \{0,1\}^m}\in\F_q^M$.
   898	
   899	\begin{lemma}
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.

   612	The following theorem records the self-testing (also known as \emph{rigidity})
   613	properties of the Magic Square game.
   614	Its self-testing properties
   615	are crucial to the Pauli basis test.
   616	In particular, it is used to enforce anticommutation relations between certain
   617	pairs of operators.
   618	We will refer to this theorem in the proof of the soundness of the Pauli basis test (\Cref{thm:pauli} below) in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}.
   619	
   620	\begin{theorem}[Rigidity of the Magic Square game]
   621	  \label{thm:ms-rigidity}
   622	
   623	
   624	Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ be a strategy that succeeds in the Magic Square game $\game^{\MS}$ with probability $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ is a state. Then there exist local isometries $\phi_A: \mH_A \to \mH_{A'} \otimes \mH_{A''},\phi_B: \mH_B \to \mH_{B'} \otimes \mH_{B''}$ (where $\mH_{A'},\mH_{B'} \cong (\C^2)^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mH_{A''},\mH_{B''}$ are finite dimensional) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{A''} \otimes \mH_{B''}$ such that 
   625	\begin{enumerate}
   626	    \item $\left \| \phi_A \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2} \otimes \ket{\aux} \right \| \leq O(\sqrt{\eps})$,
   627	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have that
   628	    \begin{gather*}
   629	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_b \otimes I_{B'B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\sigma^X_b)_{A'} \otimes I_{A'' B' B''} \\
   630	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_b \otimes I_{B'B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\sigma^Z_b)_{A'} \otimes I_{A'' B' B''} \\
   631	        I_{A'A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1}_b    \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} I_{A' A'' B''} \otimes (\sigma^X_b)_{B'} \\
   632	        I_{A'A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}_b    \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} I_{A' A'' B''} \otimes (\sigma^Z_b)_{B'}
   633	    \end{gather*}
   634	    where the $\approx_{\sqrt{\eps}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}_{A'B'} \otimes \ket{\aux}_{A''B''}$ and the answer summation is over $b \in \{0,1\}$. As a consequence, letting 
   635	    \begin{gather*}
   636	    \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} = \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_0 - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_1 \\
   637	    \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5} = \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_0 - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_1 \\
   638	    \end{gather*}
   639	    it holds that
   640	    \begin{gather*}
   641	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5} \otimes I_{B' B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}  \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} \otimes I_{B' B''} \\
   642	        I_{A' A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1} \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}  \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} - I_{A' A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}  \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1} \;,
   643	      \end{gather*}
   644	      where the notation $M \approx_{\delta} N$ for $M, N$ that are not POVM
   645	      elements means
   646	      \[  \bra{\psi} (M-N)^\dagger (M-N) \ket{\psi}  \leq  O(\delta). \]
   647	\end{enumerate}
   648	
   649	\end{theorem}
   650	\begin{proof}
   651	 	A proof of the rigidity of the Magic Square game can be found in~\cite[Theorem 6.9]{coladangelo2017robust}. There are a couple minor differences between their rigidity statement and the one stated here. First, they state that the robustness of the Magic Square self-test is $O(\eps)$; however they specify the closeness between the actual and ideal states in terms of the trace norm, whereas we specify the closeness between $\phi_\alice \otimes \phi_\bob \ket{\psi}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}\otimes \ket{\aux}$ in terms of the Euclidean distance, which translates to $O(\sqrt{\eps})$ instead of $O(\eps)$. Second, their choice of ideal strategy specifies that the observables corresponding to $\Variable_1$ and $\Variable_5$ questions are $I \otimes \sigma^Z$ and $\sigma^{Z} \sigma^{X} \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$; however under a local change of basis these are equivalent to $\sigma^X \otimes I$ and $\sigma^Z \otimes I$ respectively.
   652	\end{proof}
   653	
   654	We will need the following theorem,
   655	which shows that any pair of anticommuting observables 
   656	can be used to form a value-$1$ strategy for the Magic Square game.
   657	
   658	\begin{theorem}
   659	  \label{thm:ms-from-ac}
   660	  Let $A = \{A_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ and $B = \{B_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ be two-outcome
   661	  projective measurements acting on $(\C^q)^{\otimes n}$ which are consistent on
   662	  $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n}$, and let $\mathcal{O}_A = A_0 - A_1$ and
   663	  $\mathcal{O}_B = B_0 - B_1$ be the corresponding observables.
   664	  Suppose that $\mathcal{O}_A \mathcal{O}_B = -\mathcal{O}_B \mathcal{O}_A$.
   665	  Then there exists a symmetric strategy $\strategy = (\psi, M)$ for the Magic
   666	  Square game with the following properties.
   667	  \begin{enumerate}
   668	  \item $\strategy$ is an SPCC strategy of value $1$.
   669	  \item The state $\ket{\psi}$ has the form $\ket{\psi} = \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes
   670	      n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}$.
   671	  \item For $b \in \{0,1\}$, we have $M^{\Variable_1}_b = A_b \otimes I$ and
   672	    $M^{\Variable_5}_b = B_b \otimes I$.\label{item:embeds}
   673	  \end{enumerate}
   674	\end{theorem}
   675	
   676	\begin{proof}
   677	  The strategy~$\strategy$ is based on the canonical two-qubit strategy for the
   678	  Magic Square game as described in, for example,~\cite{aravind2002simple}.
   679	  The state is $\ket{\psi} = \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}$.
   680	  We specify the measurements of~$\strategy$ in
   681	  Figure~\ref{fig:ms-operator-soln} as an \emph{operator solution} for the Magic
   682	  Square game, meant to be read as follows: each cell contains a two-outcome
   683	  projective measurement $\{E_0, E_1\}$ on $(\C^q)^{\otimes n} \otimes \C^2$
   684	  written as its \emph{$\pm 1$-valued observable} $E_0 - E_1$.
   685	  When Player~$\alice$ or~$\bob$ receives the question $\Variable_j$ for $j \in
   686	  \{1, \ldots, 9\}$, they measure their share of~$\ket{\psi}$ using the
   687	  measurement specified by the cell corresponding to~$\Variable_j$ and receive a
   688	  single-bit measurement.
   689	  When they receive the question $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,6\}$,
   690	  they simultaneously perform the three measurements in the corresponding row or
   691	  column on $\ket{\psi}$ to obtain three bits.
   692	  For example, if Player~$\alice$ receives question~$\Variable_1$, they
   693	  measure~$\ket{\psi}$ using the measurement $\{A_0 \otimes I, A_1 \otimes I\}$
   694	  corresponding to the observable $\cal{O}_A \otimes I$ (where the first
   695	  operator acts on $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n}$ and the second acts on
   696	  $\ket{\EPR_2}$).
   697	  Similarly, on question~$\Variable_5$, they use the measurement $\{B_0 \otimes
   698	  I, B_1 \otimes I\}$.
   699	  This establishes Item~\ref{item:embeds} of the theorem.

   723	  First, we show that this gives a well-defined strategy.

    88	structure Strategy (G : Game) where
    89	  ιA : Type
    90	  ιB : Type
    91	  [ιAFintype : Fintype ιA]
    92	  [ιBFintype : Fintype ιB]
    93	  [ιADecidableEq : DecidableEq ιA]

    97	  A : G.QuestionA → Measurement G.AnswerA ιA
    98	  B : G.QuestionB → Measurement G.AnswerB ιB

   101	  Strategy.ιADecidableEq Strategy.ιBDecidableEq

   103	/-- The rectangular tensor placement used in strategy probabilities.  This is
   104	the finite-matrix realization of `def:tensor-product-strategy`, blueprint
   105	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69`; paper origin
   106	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
   107	-/
   108	def heteroKron {ιA ιB : Type*} (A : Op ιA) (B : Op ιB) : Op (ιA × ιB) :=
   109	  Matrix.kronecker A B
   110	
   111	/- The Euclidean linear map is the shared action used by the value and distance
   112	functionals.  Keeping it at the Euclidean-space level avoids accidentally
   113	using the function-space supremum norm of `Matrix.mulVec`. -/
   114	/-- Apply a finite matrix to a Euclidean-space state.  This is the Hilbert-space
   115	action underlying `def:tensor-product-value`, paper
   116	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
   117	noncomputable def applyOperatorToState {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   118	    (M : Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι :=
   119	  Matrix.toEuclideanLin M ψ

   121	/-- The Born weight of an answer pair for a strategy.  Lean-only support for
   122	`def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper
   123	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
   124	private noncomputable def outcomeWeight {G : Game} (S : Strategy G)
   125	    (x : G.QuestionA) (y : G.QuestionB) (a : G.AnswerA) (b : G.AnswerB) : ℝ :=
   126	  let M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (S.ιA × S.ιB) :=
   127	    heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) ((S.B y).effect b)
   128	  let acted := applyOperatorToState M S.ψ
   129	  (inner ℂ S.ψ acted).re
   130	
   131	/--
   132	The tensor-product value, expressed as the distribution average of the Born
   133	probabilities.  This is `def:tensor-product-value` in
   134	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, with paper origin
   135	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:40-57`.
   136	-/
   137	noncomputable def Strategy.value {G : Game} (S : Strategy G) : ℝ :=
   138	  avgOver G.μ (fun xy =>
   139	    ∑ a : G.AnswerA, ∑ b : G.AnswerB,
   140	      if G.decide xy.1 xy.2 a b then outcomeWeight S xy.1 xy.2 a b else 0)
   141	
   142	/--
   143	The tensor-product game value as a conditional supremum over all finite
   144	strategies.  The `sSup (Set.range ...)` form is the csSup formulation requested
   145	for `def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint
   146	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper origin
   147	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:40-57`; attainment is
   148	intentionally not asserted here.
   149	-/
   150	noncomputable def Game.value (G : Game) : ℝ :=
   151	  sSup (Set.range (fun S : Strategy G => S.value))
   152	
   153	end MIPStarRE.QPBT
