   404	noncomputable instance (P : AdmissibleParams) : Fintype (PauliAnswer P) :=
   405	  Fintype.ofEquiv (PauliAnswerCode P) (pauliAnswerEquiv P).symm
   406	
   407	instance (P : AdmissibleParams) : Inhabited (PauliAnswer P) :=
   408	  ⟨.bit 0⟩
   409	
   410	/-- The phase bit `γ(u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)` from `eq:gamma-value`.  It uses the
   411	fixed trace selected by `P.model`, as required by the paper's fixed
   412	self-dual-normal representation.  Blueprint
   413	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`; paper origin
   414	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1198-1212`.
   415	-/
   416	noncomputable def gammaValue (P : AdmissibleParams)
   417	    (uX uZ : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)
   418	    (rX rZ : PauliScalar P) : ZMod 2 :=
   419	  fixedBinTrace P.model
   420	    (dotProduct (rX • indicatorVec uX) (rZ • indicatorVec uZ))
   421	
   422	/-- The commutation bit attached to a full Pauli ambient question, from
   423	`eq:gamma-value` in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   424	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   425	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1198-1212`.
   426	-/
   427	noncomputable def pauliPairGamma (P : AdmissibleParams) (z : PauliSpace P) : ZMod 2 :=
   428	  gammaValue P (pauliXBlock z) (pauliZBlock z)
   429	    (pauliRXBlock z) (pauliRZBlock z)
   430	
   431	/-- The answer constructor prescribed by each Pauli question type; this is the
   432	well-formedness part of `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   433	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   434	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   435	-/
   436	def validPauliAnswer {P : AdmissibleParams} (t : PauliType) (a : PauliAnswer P) : Bool :=
   437	  match t, a with
   438	  | .point _, .value _ => true
   439	  | .aline _, .alinePoly _ => true
   440	  | .dline _, .dlinePoly _ => true
   441	  | .pauli _, .pauliOutcome _ => true
   442	  | .pairW _, .bit _ => true
   443	  | .pair, .pairBits _ => true
   444	  | .ms (.constraint _), .msTriple _ => true
   445	  | .ms (.var _), .bit _ => true
   446	  | _, _ => false
   447	
   448	/-- The axis-line versus point relation used by `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   449	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   450	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   451	-/
   452	def pauliAlinePointCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   453	    (line point : PauliSpace P) (f : Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   454	    (a : PauliScalar P) : Prop :=
   455	  -- The universal form preserves the source's zero-direction convention.
   456	  ∀ t : PauliScalar P,
   457	    pauliPointBlock W point =
   458	        pauliPointBlock W line + t • coordinateDirection
   459	          (chiIndex P.toLdParams (pauliScalarBlock line)) →
   460	      evalCoefficient f t = a
   461	
   462	/-- The diagonal-line versus point relation used by `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   463	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   464	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   465	-/
   466	def pauliDlinePointCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   467	    (line point : PauliSpace P) (f : Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   468	    (a : PauliScalar P) : Prop :=
   469	  ∀ t : PauliScalar P,
   470	    pauliPointBlock W point = pauliPointBlock W line +
   471	        t • pauliDirectionBlock line →
   472	      evalCoefficient f t = a
   473	
   474	/-- The raw Pauli-versus-point consistency relation from `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   475	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   476	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   477	-/
   478	def pauliPointPauliCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   479	    (point : PauliSpace P) (h : PauliRegister P) (a : PauliScalar P) : Prop :=
   480	  lowDegreeEnc h (pauliPointBlock W point) = a
   481	
   482	/-- The Pair/W consistency relation, including the one-sided gamma gate, from
   483	`def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   484	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   485	-/
   486	def pauliPairCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   487	    (z : PauliSpace P) (β : ZMod 2) (bits : ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) : Prop :=
   488	  pauliPairGamma P z ≠ 0 ∨
   489	    (match W with
   490	    | .X => bits.1 = β
   491	    | .Z => bits.2 = β)
   492	
   493	/-- The point/Pair/W trace consistency relation from `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   494	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   495	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   496	-/
   497	def pauliPointPairCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   498	    (z : PauliSpace P) (a : PauliScalar P) (β : ZMod 2) : Prop :=
   499	  pauliPairGamma P z ≠ 0 ∨
   500	    fixedBinTrace P.model
   501	      (a * (match W with
   502	      | .X => pauliRXBlock z
   503	      | .Z => pauliRZBlock z)) = β
   504	
   505	/-- The Point/Variable consistency clause of `def:pauli-win-predicate`.
   506	The check is gated by `gamma = 0` and only uses Variable 1 in the X basis or
   507	Variable 5 in the Z basis.  Blueprint
   508	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`; paper origin
   509	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   510	-/
   511	def pauliPointVariableCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   512	    (z : PauliSpace P) (j : Fin 9) (a : PauliScalar P) (β : ZMod 2) : Prop :=
   513	  pauliPairGamma P z = 0 ∨
   514	    (j = ⟨0, by decide⟩ ∧ W = .X ∧
   515	        fixedBinTrace P.model (a * pauliRXBlock z) = β) ∨
   516	    (j = ⟨4, by decide⟩ ∧ W = .Z ∧
   517	        fixedBinTrace P.model (a * pauliRZBlock z) = β)
   518	
   519	/-- The Pauli win predicate, with constructor-shape rejection.  This is
   520	`def:pauli-win-predicate` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`,
   521	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   522	-/
   523	noncomputable def pauliWinPredicate (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   524	    PauliQuestion P → PauliQuestion P → PauliAnswer P → PauliAnswer P → Bool :=
   525	  open Classical in
   526	  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
   527	    if validPauliAnswer tA a && validPauliAnswer tB b then
   528	      if tA = tB then
   529	        decide (a = b)
   530	      else
   531	        match tA, tB, a, b with
   532	      | .aline W, .point W', .alinePoly f, .value u =>
   533	          if W = W' then decide (pauliAlinePointCondition P W xA xB f u) else true
   534	      | .point W, .aline W', .value u, .alinePoly f =>
   535	          if W = W' then decide (pauliAlinePointCondition P W xB xA f u) else true
   536	      | .dline W, .point W', .dlinePoly f, .value u =>
   537	          if W = W' then decide (pauliDlinePointCondition P W xA xB f u) else true
   538	      | .point W, .dline W', .value u, .dlinePoly f =>
   539	          if W = W' then decide (pauliDlinePointCondition P W xB xA f u) else true
   540	      | .point W, .pauli W', .value u, .pauliOutcome h =>
   541	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPauliCondition P W xA h u) else true
   542	      | .pauli W, .point W', .pauliOutcome h, .value u =>
   543	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPauliCondition P W xB h u) else true
   544	      | .pairW W, .pair, .bit β, .pairBits bits =>
   545	          decide (pauliPairCondition P W xA β bits)
   546	      | .pair, .pairW W, .pairBits bits, .bit β =>
   547	          decide (pauliPairCondition P W xB β bits)
   548	      | .point W, .pairW W', .value u, .bit β =>
   549	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPairCondition P W xB u β) else true
   550	      | .pairW W, .point W', .bit β, .value u =>
   551	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPairCondition P W xA u β) else true
   552	      | .ms (.constraint i), .ms (.var j), .msTriple β, .bit γ =>
   553	          if ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j then
   554	            decide (pauliPairGamma P xA = 0 ∨
   555	              msWinPredicate (.constraint i) (.var j) (.triple β) (.bit γ))
   556	          else true
   557	      | .ms (.var j), .ms (.constraint i), .bit γ, .msTriple β =>
   558	          if ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j then
   559	            decide (pauliPairGamma P xB = 0 ∨
   560	              msWinPredicate (.var j) (.constraint i) (.bit γ) (.triple β))
   561	          else true
   562	      | .point W, .ms (.var j), .value u, .bit β =>
   563	          decide (pauliPointVariableCondition P W xB j u β)
   564	      | .ms (.var j), .point W, .bit β, .value u =>
   565	          decide (pauliPointVariableCondition P W xA j u β)
   566	        | _, _, _, _ => true
   567	    else false
   568	
   569	/-- The Pauli basis test game.  This is `def:pauli-question-distribution` and
   570	`def:pauli-win-predicate` packaged as the symmetric game of
   571	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-367`, paper origin
   572	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1225`.
   573	-/
   574	noncomputable def pauliBasisTest (P : AdmissibleParams) : Game where
   575	  QuestionA := PauliQuestion P
   576	  QuestionB := PauliQuestion P
   577	  AnswerA := PauliAnswer P
   578	  AnswerB := PauliAnswer P
   579	  μ := pauliQuestionDistribution P
   580	  μ_prob := by sorry
   581	  decide := pauliWinPredicate P
   582	
   583	end

   263	/-- A finite edge set for the typed Pauli question graph.  The self-loops and
   264	the displayed type-incidence families are the graph used by the sampler in
   265	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint lines 285-329, paper origin
   266	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   267	-/
   268	def pauliEdges : Finset (Sym2 PauliType) :=
   269	  let loops := Finset.univ.image (fun t : PauliType => Sym2.mk t t)
   270	  let lineEdges :=
   271	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   272	      Sym2.mk (.point W) (.aline W)) ∪
   273	      (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   274	        Sym2.mk (.point W) (.dline W)) ∪
   275	      (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   276	        Sym2.mk (.point W) (.pauli W))
   277	  let basisEdges :=
   278	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   279	      Sym2.mk (.point W) (.pairW W)) ∪
   280	      ({Sym2.mk (.point .X) (.ms (.var ⟨0, by decide⟩)),
   281	        Sym2.mk (.point .Z) (.ms (.var ⟨4, by decide⟩))} : Finset (Sym2 PauliType))
   282	  let pairEdges :=
   283	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   284	      Sym2.mk (.pairW W) .pair)
   285	  let msEdges' :=
   286	    (Finset.univ : Finset (MsType × MsType)).filter (fun xy =>
   287	      Sym2.mk xy.1 xy.2 ∈ msEdges) |>.image (fun xy =>
   288	        Sym2.mk (.ms xy.1) (.ms xy.2))
   289	  loops ∪ lineEdges ∪ basisEdges ∪ pairEdges ∪ msEdges'
   290	
   291	/-- A Pauli question is a type together with a full ambient coefficient vector
   292	(`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper
   293	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`).

   295	abbrev PauliQuestion (P : AdmissibleParams) := PauliType × PauliSpace P

   297	/-- The ordered-edge subtype used by the Pauli question sampler.  This is
   298	the finite carrier underlying `graphDistribution pauliEdges`; it is Lean-only
   299	infrastructure for `def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint
   300	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   301	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.

   303	abbrev PauliEdge :=
   304	  {e : PauliType × PauliType // Sym2.mk e.1 e.2 ∈ pauliEdges}
   305	
   306	/-- The Pauli graph has a loop, so its ordered-edge subtype is nonempty.  This
   307	is a finite-carrier fact used only to instantiate the uniform source sampler
   308	for `def:pauli-question-distribution`; the graph itself is the source-facing
   309	object `pauliEdges` above (same blueprint and paper references).

   311	theorem pauliEdge_nonempty : Nonempty PauliEdge := by
   312	  refine ⟨⟨(.point .X, .point .X), ?_⟩⟩
   313	  simp [pauliEdges]

   335	inductive PauliAnswer (P : AdmissibleParams) where
   336	  | value (a : PauliScalar P)

   339	  | pairBits (a : ZMod 2 × ZMod 2)
   340	  | bit (a : ZMod 2)
   341	  | msTriple (a : Fin 3 → ZMod 2)
   342	  | pauliOutcome (a : PauliRegister P)

   345	/-- A finite sum code used only to construct the `Fintype` instance for the

   350	abbrev PauliAnswerCode (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   351	  PauliScalar P ⊕
   352	    ((Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
   353	      ((Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
   354	        ((ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) ⊕
   355	          (ZMod 2 ⊕ ((Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ PauliRegister P)))))

   366	    | .alinePoly a => .inr (.inl a)
   367	    | .dlinePoly a => .inr (.inr (.inl a))
   368	    | .pairBits a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))
   369	    | .bit a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))
   370	    | .msTriple a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))))
   371	    | .pauliOutcome a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr a)))))
   372	  invFun
   373	    | .inl a => .value a
   374	    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePoly a
   375	    | .inr (.inr (.inl a)) => .dlinePoly a
   376	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))) => .pairBits a
   377	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))) => .bit a
   378	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))) => .msTriple a
   379	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr a))))) => .pauliOutcome a
   380	  left_inv := by

   382	    cases x <;> rfl

   387	    | inr x =>
   388	        cases x with
   389	        | inl a => rfl
   390	        | inr x =>
   391	            cases x with
   392	            | inl a => rfl
   393	            | inr x =>
   394	                cases x with
   395	                | inl a => rfl
   396	                | inr x =>
   397	                    cases x with
   398	                    | inl a => rfl
   399	                    | inr x =>
   400	                        cases x with
   401	                        | inl a => rfl
   402	                        | inr a => rfl

   423	`eq:gamma-value` in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   424	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   425	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1198-1212`.
   426	-/
   427	noncomputable def pauliPairGamma (P : AdmissibleParams) (z : PauliSpace P) : ZMod 2 :=
   428	  gammaValue P (pauliXBlock z) (pauliZBlock z)
   429	    (pauliRXBlock z) (pauliRZBlock z)
   430

     4	/-!
     5	# The Magic Square game
     6	
     7	The Magic Square component is represented by finite constraint and variable
     8	question types, the incidence graph, and the two corresponding answer forms.
     9	Its rigidity theorem is outside the stage-4.1 statement closure; only the game
    10	carrier is needed here.
    11	
    12	## References
    13	
    14	This file formalizes `def:ms-game` in
    15	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, from
    16	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    17	-/
    18	
    19	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    20	
    21	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    22	
    23	/-- A Magic Square question is either a row/column constraint or a cell
    24	variable.  This is `def:ms-game`, blueprint lines 188-203, paper origin
    25	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    26	-/
    27	inductive MsType where
    28	  | constraint (i : Fin 6)
    29	  | var (j : Fin 9)
    30	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    31	
    32	/-- The cell incident to a constraint and one of its three positions in
    33	`def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    34	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    35	-/
    36	def msConstraintVars (i : Fin 6) (j : Fin 3) : Fin 9 :=
    37	  ⟨if i.val < 3 then i.val * 3 + j.val else i.val - 3 + j.val * 3, by
    38	    by_cases h : i.val < 3 <;> simp [h] <;> omega⟩
    39	
    40	/-- The exceptional Magic Square parity, equal to one only on the final
    41	constraint.  Blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`; paper
    42	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    43	-/
    44	def msParity (i : Fin 6) : ZMod 2 :=
    45	  if i.val = 5 then 1 else 0
    46	
    47	/-- The 18 constraint-variable incidence edges of the Magic Square graph in
    48	`def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    49	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    50	-/
    51	def msEdges : Finset (Sym2 MsType) :=
    52	  (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin 6 × Fin 3)).image (fun ij =>
    53	    Sym2.mk (.constraint ij.1) (.var (msConstraintVars ij.1 ij.2)))
    54	
    55	/-- The Magic Square incidence graph has an edge, as required by the
    56	nonempty-support API of `graphDistribution`.  This is the finite carrier fact
    57	used to instantiate `def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`,
    58	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    59	-/
    60	theorem msEdges_nonempty : msEdges.Nonempty := by
    61	  refine ⟨Sym2.mk (.constraint 0) (.var (msConstraintVars 0 0)), ?_⟩
    62	  exact Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨(0, 0), Finset.mem_univ _, rfl⟩
    63	
    64	/-- A Magic Square answer is a parity triple or a single cell bit, as prescribed
    65	by `def:ms-game`, blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`,
    66	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    67	-/
    68	inductive MsAnswer where
    69	  | triple (β : Fin 3 → ZMod 2)
    70	  | bit (γ : ZMod 2)
    71	  deriving DecidableEq
    72	
    73	/-- A finite code for the two Magic Square answer constructors.  This is
    74	Lean-only carrier infrastructure for `def:ms-game`, blueprint
    75	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    76	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    77	-/
    78	abbrev MsAnswerCode := (Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ ZMod 2
    79	
    80	/-- The constructor-preserving code equivalence for `MsAnswer`; Lean-only
    81	finite-carrier infrastructure for `def:ms-game`, blueprint
    82	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    83	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    84	-/
    85	noncomputable def msAnswerEquiv : MsAnswer ≃ MsAnswerCode where
    86	  toFun
    87	    | .triple β => .inl β
    88	    | .bit γ => .inr γ
    89	  invFun
    90	    | .inl β => .triple β
    91	    | .inr γ => .bit γ
    92	  left_inv := by intro x; cases x <;> rfl
    93	  right_inv := by
    94	    intro x
    95	    cases x <;> rfl
    96	
    97	noncomputable instance : Fintype MsAnswer :=
    98	  Fintype.ofEquiv MsAnswerCode msAnswerEquiv.symm
    99	
   100	instance : Inhabited MsAnswer := ⟨.bit 0⟩
   101	
   102	/-- The Magic Square consistency predicate.  Constructor mismatches are
   103	rejected, as required by `def:ms-game` (blueprint lines 188-203; paper
   104	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`).
   105	-/
   106	def msWinPredicate :
   107	    MsType → MsType → MsAnswer → MsAnswer → Bool
   108	  | .constraint i, .constraint j, .triple β, .triple β' =>
   109	      decide (i = j ∧ β = β')
   110	  | .var i, .var j, .bit γ, .bit γ' =>
   111	      decide (i = j ∧ γ = γ')
   112	  | .constraint i, .var j, .triple β, .bit γ =>
   113	      decide
   114	        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
   115	          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
   116	  | .var j, .constraint i, .bit γ, .triple β =>
   117	      decide
   118	        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
   119	          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
   120	  | _, _, _, _ => false
   121	
   122	/-- The Magic Square game as a finite `Game`.  This is `def:ms-game` in
   123	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
   124	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
   125	-/
   126	noncomputable def msGame : Game where
   127	  QuestionA := MsType
   128	  QuestionB := MsType
   129	  AnswerA := MsAnswer
   130	  AnswerB := MsAnswer
   131	  μ := graphDistribution msEdges msEdges_nonempty
   132	  μ_prob := by sorry
   133	  decide := msWinPredicate
   134	
   135	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     6	/-!
     7	# The Pauli basis test
     8	
     9	This file supplies the finite question and answer alphabets, the typed
    10	conditionally-linear question sampler, and the Boolean win predicate for the
    11	Pauli basis test.  The quantitative soundness theorem is isolated in
    12	`Soundness.lean`.

    14	## References
    15	
    16	The source-facing nodes are `def:admissible`, `def:pauli-question-distribution`,

    22	open scoped BigOperators
    23	
    24	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    25	
    26	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    27	
    28	noncomputable section
    29	
    30	/-- The numerical admissible Pauli-test parameter package.  Its scalar carrier
    31	uses the once-and-for-all model `fixedFieldModel q hq`, so the paper's fixed
    32	self-dual-normal identification is not quantified in the test statement.  This
    33	is `def:admissible` in
    34	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-283`, paper origin

    36	-/
    37	structure AdmissibleParams where
    38	  q : ℕ
    39	  m : ℕ
    40	  d : ℕ
    41	  hd : 1 ≤ d
    42	  hq : IsAdmissibleSize q
    43	  hdvd : m ∣ q
    44	
    45	/-- The positivity of the ambient dimension is a proof obligation implicit in
    46	the admissibility convention `def:admissible`, blueprint
    47	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-283`, paper origin
    48	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
    49	-/
    50	theorem AdmissibleParams.one_le_m (P : AdmissibleParams) : 1 ≤ P.m := by
    51	  sorry
    52	
    53	/-- The fixed model accessor for an admissible parameter package.  It is a
    54	compatibility view of the global `fixedFieldModel` selector, not an independently
    55	quantified field representation.  Blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-283`; paper
    56	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
    57	-/
    58	noncomputable def AdmissibleParams.model (P : AdmissibleParams) : FixedFieldModel P.q :=
    59	  fixedFieldModel P.q P.hq
    60	
    61	/-- The low-degree parameter view of an admissible Pauli-test package.  This is
    62	a Lean-only bridge supporting the statement closure; it is not an additional
    63	hypothesis of `thm:pauli`.  Blueprint
    64	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`, paper origin
    65	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
    66	-/
    67	def AdmissibleParams.toLdParams (P : AdmissibleParams) : LdParams where
    68	  q := P.q
    69	  m := P.m
    70	  d := P.d
    71	  k := 1
    72	  hm := P.one_le_m
    73	  hd := P.hd
    74	  hk := by decide
    75	  hq := P.hq
    76	  hdvd := P.hdvd
    77	
    78	/-- The scalar carrier associated with an admissible parameter package.  It is
    79	the globally fixed field carrier selected by `AdmissibleParams.model` in
    80	`def:admissible`, blueprint
    81	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-283`, paper origin
    82	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
    83	-/
    84	abbrev PauliScalar (P : AdmissibleParams) := P.model.K
    85	
    86	/-- The six families of Pauli-test questions.  This is part of
    87	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
    88	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
    89	-/
    90	inductive PauliType where
    91	  | point (W : PauliKind)
    92	  | aline (W : PauliKind)
    93	  | dline (W : PauliKind)
    94	  | pauli (W : PauliKind)
    95	  | pairW (W : PauliKind)
    96	  | pair
    97	  | ms (t : MsType)
    98	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    99	
   100	/-- The register blocks used by the Pauli question space.  These are the
   101	coordinates displayed in `def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint
   102	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   103	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   104	-/
   105	abbrev PauliIndex (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   106	  (((((Fin P.m ⊕ Fin P.m) ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Fin P.m) ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Unit)
   107	
   108	/-- The ambient Pauli question coefficient space (`def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   109	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper origin
   110	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`).
   111	-/
   112	abbrev PauliSpace (P : AdmissibleParams) := PauliIndex P → PauliScalar P
   113	
   114	/-- The coefficient register indexed by the Boolean cube in
   115	`def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
   116	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:908-945`.
   117	-/
   118	abbrev PauliRegister (P : AdmissibleParams) := Cube P.m → PauliScalar P
   119	
   120	/- The nested sum is the fixed register order
   121	`V_X ⊕ V_Z ⊕ V_I ⊕ V_V ⊕ V_{R_X} ⊕ V_{R_Z}` from the blueprint. -/
   122	/-- The `V_X` block of an ambient Pauli vector (`def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   123	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper origin
   124	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`). -/
   125	def pauliXBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   126	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl i)))))
   127	
   128	/-- The `V_Z` block of an ambient Pauli vector in `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   129	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   130	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   131	-/
   132	def pauliZBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   133	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr i)))))
   134	
   135	/-- The scalar block `V_I` of an ambient Pauli vector in
   136	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   137	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   138	-/
   139	def pauliScalarBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
   140	  z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr ()))))
   141	
   142	/-- The direction block `V_V` of an ambient Pauli vector in
   143	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   144	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   145	-/
   146	def pauliDirectionBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   147	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inr i)))
   148	
   149	/-- The `r_X` scalar block in the Pauli question content from
   150	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   151	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   152	-/
   153	def pauliRXBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
   154	  z (.inl (.inr ()))
   155	
   156	/-- The `r_Z` scalar block in the Pauli question content from
   157	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   158	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   159	-/
   160	def pauliRZBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
   161	  z (.inr ())
   162	
   163	/-- Select the basis-dependent point block from a Pauli question content in
   164	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   165	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   166	-/
   167	def pauliPointBlock {P : AdmissibleParams} (W : PauliKind) (z : PauliSpace P) :
   168	    Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   169	  match W with
   170	  | .X => pauliXBlock z
   171	  | .Z => pauliZBlock z
   172	
   173	/-- Read the low-degree register selected by a basis from an ambient Pauli
   174	vector.  Lean-only coordinate plumbing for `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   175	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   176	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   177	-/
   178	def pauliToLd (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind) (z : PauliSpace P) :
   179	    LdSpace P.toLdParams :=
   180	  fun i => match i with
   181	  | .inl (.inl j) => pauliPointBlock W z j
   182	  | .inl (.inr _) => pauliScalarBlock z
   183	  | .inr j => pauliDirectionBlock z j
   184	
   185	/-- Embed a low-degree vector into the basis-selected Pauli blocks, clearing the
   186	other basis and the two `r` registers.  This is Lean-only coordinate plumbing
   187	for `def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint
   188	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   189	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   190	-/
   191	def embedLd (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   192	    (u : LdSpace P.toLdParams) : PauliSpace P :=
   193	  fun i => match i with
   194	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))) =>
   195	      match W with
   196	      | .X => u (.inl (.inl j))
   197	      | .Z => 0
   198	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))) =>
   199	      match W with
   200	      | .X => 0
   201	      | .Z => u (.inl (.inl j))
   202	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inr _))) => u (.inl (.inr ()))
   203	  | .inl (.inl (.inr j)) => u (.inr j)
   204	  | .inl (.inr _) => 0
   205	  | .inr _ => 0
   206	
   207	/-- The type-4 projection retaining `V_X`, `V_Z`, `V_{R_X}`, and `V_{R_Z}` from
   208	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper
   209	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   210	-/
   211	def pauliSharedProjection {P : AdmissibleParams} (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliSpace P :=
   212	  fun i => match i with
   213	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))) => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))))
   214	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))) => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))))
   215	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inr _))) => 0
   216	  | .inl (.inl (.inr _)) => 0
   217	  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
   218	  | .inr _ => z (.inr ())
   219	
   220	/-- The source level attached to each typed Pauli CL map.  This records the
   221	exact levels in items 1--5 of `def:pauli-question-distribution`: point, line,
   222	and diagonal maps have levels 1, 2, and 3, the Pauli map has level 0, and the
   223	shared projection has level 1.  Blueprint
   224	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper origin
   225	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   226	-/
   227	def pauliCLLevel : PauliType → ℕ
   228	  | .point _ => 1
   229	  | .aline _ => 2
   230	  | .dline _ => 3
   231	  | .pauli _ => 0
   232	  | .pairW _ => 1
   233	  | .pair => 1
   234	  | .ms _ => 1
   235	
   236	/-- The typed CL dispatcher.  The point/line maps are the corresponding
   237	low-degree maps embedded in the selected basis block; Pair, Magic Square, and
   238	Pair/W types use the shared projection; Pauli/W is the zero-level map.  This
   239	is the direct finite-space form of `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   240	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin

   151	## (d) Statement sketch of `MIPStarRE.QPBT.pauli_soundness`
   152	
   153	```lean
   154	/-- Soundness function of the Pauli basis test; argument order (ε, m, d, q)
   155	everywhere, per rem:delta-qld-argument-order. Real rpow throughout. -/
   156	noncomputable def deltaQld (a b ε : ℝ) (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
   157	  a * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) ^ a *
   158	    (ε ^ b + (q : ℝ) ^ (-b) + (2 : ℝ) ^ (-(b * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ))))
   159	
   160	/-- thm:pauli (qpbt-paper 08_…tex:1426-1447): soundness of the Pauli basis test. -/
   161	theorem pauli_soundness :
   162	    ∃ a b : ℝ, 1 ≤ a ∧ 0 < b ∧ b < 1 ∧
   163	      ∀ (P : AdmissibleParams) [FieldModel P.q] (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε →
   164	        ∀ S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P), 1 - ε ≤ S.value →
   165	          ∃ (ιA' ιB' : Type) (_ : Fintype ιA') (_ : DecidableEq ιA')
   166	            (_ : Fintype ιB') (_ : DecidableEq ιB')
   167	            (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   168	                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P))
   169	            (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   170	                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
   171	            (aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')), ‖aux‖ = 1 ∧
   172	            -- item 1: ‖φA ⊗ φB ψ − aux ⊗ EPR_q^{⊗M}‖ ≤ δ_qld  (squared distance,
   173	            -- via stateDistSq and deltaQld²; or state with ‖·‖ directly — either
   174	            -- form is acceptable, document the choice)
   175	            ‖isometryTensor φA φB S.ψ - idealState P aux‖
   176	                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
   177	            -- item 2, for both players and both bases, summation over u ∈ F_q^M,
   178	            -- w.r.t. the ideal state; O(·) constants absorbed into a (see (e)8)
   179	            ∀ W : PauliKind,
   180	              (∑ u : PauliRegister P,
   181	                ‖(heteroKron
   182	                    (conjIsometry φA ((S.A (pauliQuestion P W)).effect
   183	                      (PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u) ...decoded))
   184	                    (1 : Op (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
   185	                  - pauliProjOnA'' P W u).mulVec (idealState P aux)‖ ^ 2)
   186	                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
   187	              (symmetric B-side bound)
   188	```
   189	
   190	Supporting definitions in Soundness.lean (all NEW, Lean-only):
   191	`idealState P aux := reindexState prodShuffle (vecTensor aux (eprState (PauliRegister P)))`;
   192	`pauliQuestion P W : (pauliBasisTest P).QuestionA := (PauliType.pauli W, 0)` (the
   193	`(Pauli, W)` question has content `0`, image of the 0-level CL function);
   194	`pauliProjOnA'' P W u : Op ((ιA' × Reg) × (ιB' × Reg))` places `pauliProj W u` on the
   195	`A''` factor, identity elsewhere (and the `B''` analogue). The A-side measurement
   196	outcome family is the sub-family of `S.A` at outcomes `PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u`
   197	(other constructors carry no mass in the ideal comparison; define the family by
   198	pattern-matching `PauliAnswer → Op` with `0` on the other constructors — this is the
   199	faithful reading of "answer summation over `u ∈ F_q^M`").

   201	## (e) Settled encoding decisions (do not re-derive)
   202	
   203	1. **Polynomials — representative convention** (issue #0004, `def:polynomials-degree`):
   204	   polynomial-valued objects are representatives, not function classes. Reuse
   205	   `MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc` where a polynomial *class* is quantified.
   206	   Game *answers* are finite coefficient tuples exactly as printed in the paper
   207	   ("given by its d+1 coefficients"): `Fin (d+1) → K`, resp. `Fin (m*d+1) → K`.
   208	   Do not reuse `LDT.AxisLinePolynomial`/`DiagonalLineAnswer` (the LDT diagonal answer
   209	   is function-encoded and `Parameters`-bundled; a bridge can come later).
   210	   `def:ld-meas`/`PolyMeas` are NOT in this closure — do not build them now.
   211	2. **Distributions — match LDT, not PMF**: the LDT question distributions use
   212	   `MIPStarRE.LDT.Distribution` (Finset-supported, real weights, `Error := ℝ`) with

1	# MIPStarRE-local convention addenda
     2	
     3	The canonical convention documents live in the `lean-conventions` skill of
     4	[texra-ai/texra-lean-skills](https://github.com/texra-ai/texra-lean-skills)
     5	(auto-installed for Claude Code sessions via `.claude/settings.json`; other
     6	agents: clone the repository and symlink the skill directories, per its
     7	README). This file holds only
     8	MIPStarRE's project-local facts — it restates no shared rule, and shared
     9	rules never move here.
    10	
    11	## Style (MATHLIB_style)
    12	
    13	### Linter warnings
    14	
    15	Do not mask linter warnings instead of fixing them. A cleanup PR should not add
    16	broad `set_option linter.<name> false` blocks, and especially not file-wide
    17	blocks, just to make the build output quieter. Linters exist to expose real
    18	maintenance problems; hiding them makes later proof work and review harder.
    19	
    20	Fix the warning at its source whenever possible:
    21	
    22	- wrap long lines rather than disabling `linter.style.longLine`;
    23	- remove or narrow unused variables, section variables, and unused typeclass
    24	  assumptions rather than disabling the corresponding unused-* linter;
    25	- remove unused `simp` arguments rather than disabling `linter.unusedSimpArgs`;
    26	- rewrite proof terms or state the simplified goal explicitly rather than
    27	  silencing `linter.flexible`.
    28	
    29	If a linter warning is a genuine false positive or a temporary porting
    30	exception, use the narrowest possible scope, preferably
    31	`set_option linter.<name> false in <decl>`, and add a short nearby explanation.
    32	Such exceptions should be rare and reviewable. Never use linter suppression as
    33	the main mechanism for a linter-warning cleanup PR.
    34	
    35	## PR review (MATHLIB_pr-review)
    36	
    37	### Source-faithfulness checks
    38	
    39	For this repository, the first review question is whether a paper-facing Lean
    40	statement still represents the cited result in `references/ldt-paper/`.  Before
    41	applying the general mathlib review checklist in the lean-conventions
    42	`MATHLIB_pr-review` reference, compare every changed
    43	source-labelled theorem, lemma, proposition, corollary, or definition with the
    44	corresponding paper statement and the active blueprint entry.
    45	
    46	Reject a paper-facing statement if it has acquired a non-paper bridge, residual,
    47	repair, package, producer, proof-obligation, assumptions-bundle, hypotheses-bundle,
    48	or arbitrary implication hypothesis.  Necessary boundary hypotheses, such as
    49	positivity for division or nonemptiness of a finite type, may be faithful formal
    50	encodings of implicit paper assumptions, but they should be documented when
    51	mathematically load-bearing.
    52	
    53	Reviewers should also inspect `\lean{}` and `\leanok` links.  A source-labelled
    54	blueprint entry should point to the source theorem or its faithful construction
    55	theorem, not to conditional helpers whose assumptions are proof obligations.
    56	Auxiliary Lean declarations may be recorded in a separate remark, provided the
    57	remark states that they are not additional hypotheses in the paper theorem.
    58	
    59	## Proof integrity (PROOF_INTEGRITY)
    60	
    61	### Companion document
    62	
    63	> **Companion document:** [`anti_patterns.md`](./anti_patterns.md) catalogues
    64	> subtler proof-evasion patterns that pass every blocker check in the
    65	> lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference yet still
    66	> fail to prove the claimed mathematics (conclusion-shaped hypotheses,
    67	> definitional sleight-of-hand, zero-fallback branches, trivial default
    68	> witnesses, Mathlib-bypass castles, external `*Statement` smuggles).
    69	> Consult it alongside this file during review.
    70	
    71	### Project paper-realignment protocol
    72	
    73	The canonical paper-realignment exception in the lean-conventions
    74	`PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference is instantiated here as
    75	follows (the protocol and the `**Unfaithful:**` marker are described in
    76	`AGENTS.md`):
    77	
    78	> **Paper-realignment exception:** When a PR is explicitly realigning a
    79	> source-labelled declaration with `references/ldt-paper/`, the `sorry`
    80	> blocker of the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference may be
    81	> temporarily relaxed for the affected proof bodies.  The
    82	> PR must restore the source-faithful public statement, name the remaining proof
    83	> obligation as a theorem or lemma, and cite the paper passage plus the
    84	> tracking issue or paper-gap note.  A theorem whose proof still depends on a
    85	> known non-paper bridge, residual, repair input, obligation structure, or
    86	> conditional helper
    87	> must carry the `**Unfaithful:**` docstring marker described in `AGENTS.md`.
    88	> Review such PRs against statement faithfulness and the documented discharge
    89	> plan, not merely against the temporary `sorry` count.
    90	
    91	### Axiom policy
    92	
    93	When an external mathematical result must remain unformalized temporarily,
    94	prefer a caller-supplied `Prop` hypothesis over a global `axiom`
    95	declaration, and add a regression check (for example a
    96	`Lean.collectAxioms`-based assertion, as in
    97	`MIPStarRE.LDT.Test.AxiomAudit`) so later refactors cannot silently widen
    98	the axiomatic base.
    99	
   100	This preference does not license proposition inputs on source-labelled paper
   101	theorems.  If the cited paper theorem does not assume the proposition, a
   102	caller-supplied `Prop` hypothesis is an additional theorem hypothesis, not a
   103	proof of the paper statement.  Use such hypotheses only for explicitly
   104	conditional auxiliary results, and keep the source-labelled theorem statement
   105	faithful to the paper.
   106	
   107	### Scaffolding that blocks real formalization
   108	
   109	This is a subtle but critical failure mode: **scaffolding definitions or
   110	theorem statements that do not faithfully represent the actual mathematics**,
   111	making them impossible to connect to real Mathlib-based proofs.
   112	
   113	Signs to watch for:
   114	
   115	- Custom type definitions for objects that already exist in Mathlib (e.g.,
   116	  defining a custom `Measurement` type instead of using Mathlib's
   117	  `MeasureTheory` or operator algebra API)
   118	- Theorem statements whose hypotheses or conclusions use project-local types
   119	  that are not definitionally equal to or coercible from the Mathlib versions
   120	- Scaffolded definitions that compile but encode the wrong mathematical
   121	  semantics (e.g., a "projective measurement" definition that does not enforce
   122	  the correct positivity or completeness conditions)
   123	- Intermediate lemmas stated in terms of scaffolding types that cannot be
   124	  connected upstream to Mathlib's API without reproving everything
   125	- Definitions that "work" for `sorry`-based proofs but fail when you try to
   126	  fill in real proofs using Mathlib lemmas (type mismatches, missing instances,
   127	  incompatible universes)
   128	
   129	When reviewing scaffolded code, ask: **Can a real proof be built on top of
   130	this?** If the types, instances, and API surface don't align with Mathlib, the
   131	scaffolding is actively harmful — it creates technical debt that blocks
   132	progress rather than enabling it.
   133	
   134	### Paper-labelled theorem statement drift
   135	
   136	A theorem advertised as the Lean formalization of a paper theorem is a blocker
   137	if its public statement has drifted from the cited paper statement.
   138	Changing a theorem away from the statement in `references/ldt-paper/` is
   139	strongly discouraged unless it is forced by faithful formal encoding or by a
   140	documented mathematical necessity.
   141	
   142	The most common failure mode is replacing an unformalized proof step by an
   143	extra hypothesis on the theorem itself.  This produces a true conditional
   144	theorem, but it is not the theorem stated in the paper.  In particular, do not
   145	repair a theorem such as `mainFormal` by adding assumptions named
   146	`BridgeHypotheses`, `Input`, `Residual`, `Package`, `RepairInput`, `Producer`,
   147	generic `Hypotheses` or `Assumptions` bundles, or similar, unless those
   148	assumptions are explicitly present in the cited paper statement.
   149	
   150	Conditional helpers are a last-resort quarantine for proof work that cannot yet
   151	be closed.  Before introducing one, state the missing intermediate fact as a
   152	named lemma or theorem to be proved from the paper hypotheses.  A conditional
   153	helper is permitted only when it has a paper-gap note or tracking issue, a named
   154	obligation-discharger target, and an explicit removal plan.  Its name must show
   155	that it is conditional, for example with `_of_...`, `_assuming_...`, or
   156	`conditional...`.  It must not be the declaration used by a source-labelled
   157	blueprint theorem with `\leanok`.
   158	
   159	Existing bridge hypotheses should be treated as proof debt.  Mine their proofs
   160	for reusable arguments, but do not keep a paper-labelled theorem in a
   161	strengthened form merely because the conditional version compiles.  If the
   162	bridge data cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the correct repair is
   163	to restore the paper-aligned theorem statement and leave the missing proof as a
   164	tracked `sorry`, rather than to keep the extra assumption on the theorem.
   165	
   166	Not every explicit Lean hypothesis is statement drift.  Side conditions needed
   167	to encode the paper's domain, such as nonemptiness, decidability, field-model
   168	instances, positivity of parameters, or denominator nonvanishing, may be
   169	faithful when the paper uses the corresponding objects without comment.  These
   170	conditions should still be reviewed.  The issue is whether the hypothesis is
   171	mathematical domain data implicit in the source, or an unproved intermediate
   172	step of the source proof.
   173	
   174	For every paper-labelled theorem change, require a statement integrity audit:
   175	
   176	- paper assumptions versus Lean assumptions;
   177	- paper conclusion versus Lean conclusion;
   178	- verdict: exact, faithful boundary hypotheses, extra assumptions, weakened
   179	  conclusion, or strengthened conclusion.
   180	
   181	### Source-statement proof gaps
   182	
   183	**For source-statement proof gaps**: Read
   184	[`paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex`](paper-gaps/proof-gap-protocol.tex) when a
   185	proof is blocked by a bridge, residual, repair, input, package, or obligation
   186	structure.  It explains when to introduce an internal obligation theorem, why
   187	conditional helpers are exceptional temporary quarantine objects, and why a
   188	tracked `sorry` is preferable to a strengthened source theorem statement.

    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,

   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.

   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.

   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.

   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.

   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.

   198	Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
   199	rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
   200	mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
   201	the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
   202	discussion.

   204	\section{Form of the Note}
   205	
   206	Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
   207	source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
   208	original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
   209	be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
   210	recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
   211	serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
   212	around the mathematical assertion and its proof.
   213	
   214	The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
   215	measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
   216	should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
   217	state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
   218	be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
