   235	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}_A \otimes \cal{H}_B$ be a quantum state, and for

   243	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_{a\ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^x_b \ket{\psi}
   244	    = O(\delta)\;.\footnote{Here the use of the $O(\cdot)$ notation refers to the fact that the notation will often be used to measure consistency for \emph{famillies} of POVM and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n\in \mathbb{N}$, which will always be clear from context but omitted for legibility, see Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}.    231	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]
   232	  A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
   233	  subset of the standard basis of $V$.\footnote{The use of the term ``register''
   234	    is meant to create an analogy for how the space of multiple qubits is often

   236	  We often represent such a subspace as an indicator vector $u\in \{0,1\}^s$,
   237	  where $s=\dim(V)$, such that if $\{\hat{e}_1,\ldots,\hat{e}_s\}$ is the standard basis of
   238	  $V$ then $S = \text{span}\{\hat{e}_i|\,u_i=1\}$.
   239	\end{definition}

   241	\begin{definition}
   242	  Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_i\}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$.
   243	  For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$, $v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V$,
   244	  define the \emph{dot product}
   245	  \begin{equation*}
   246	    u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
   247	  \end{equation*}
   248	  Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. The \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
   249	  \begin{equation*}
   250	    S^\perp \,=\, \big\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0
   251	    \text{ for all }  v \in S \big\}\;.
   252	  \end{equation*}
   253	  Although the notation $S^\perp$ does not explicitly refer to $V$, the ambient
   254	  space will always be clear from context.

   256	
   257	We note that over finite fields, the notion of orthogonality does not possess
   258	all of the same intuitive properties of orthogonality over fields such as $\R$
   259	or $\C$; for example, a non-zero subspace $S$ may be orthogonal to itself (e.g.\
   260	$\mathrm{span} \{ (1,1) \}$ over $\F_2$).
   261	However, the following remains true over all fields.
   262	
   263	\begin{lemma}
   264	  \label{lem:perp_perp}
   265	  Suppose $S$ is a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) =
   266	  \dim(V)$, and 
   267	  \begin{equation*}
   268	    (S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
   269	  \end{equation*}

   272	\begin{proof}
   273	  The statement about the dimensions follows from the fact that vectors in $S^\perp$ are
   274	  the solution to a feasible linear system of equations with $\dim(S)$ linearly
   275	  independent rows; this implies that the solution space has dimension exactly
   276	  $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$.
   277	  Next, we argue that $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   278	  Let $u \in S$.
   279	  Since all vectors $v \in S^\perp$ are orthogonal to every vector in $S$,
   280	  in particular $u$, this implies that $u \in (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   281	  By dimension counting, it follows that $(S^\perp)^\perp = S$.
   282	\end{proof}
   283	
   284	\begin{definition}\label{def:complementary}
   285	  Given a linear space $V$, two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of $V$ are said to form a
   286	  pair of \emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
   287	\begin{equation*}
   288	  S \cap T = \{ 0 \}, \quad S + T = V\;.
   289	\end{equation*}
   290	In this case, we write $V = S \oplus T$.
   291	Any $x\in V$ can be written as $x = x^S + x^T$ for $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$
   292	in a unique way.
   293	We refer to $x^S$ (resp.~$x^T$) as the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel
   294	  to $T$} (resp.~\emph{onto $T$ parallel to $S$}).
   295	We call the unique linear map $L: V \to V$ that maps $x \mapsto x^S$ the
   296	\emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
   297	\end{definition}
   298	
   299	A given subspace may have many different complementary subspaces: consider the
   300	example of $S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1) \}$ in $\F_2^2$.
   301	Different complementary subspaces include $T = \mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and
   302	$T' = \mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$.
   303	It is convenient to define the notion of a \emph{canonical complement} of a
   304	subspace $S$, given a basis for $S$.
   305	
   306	\begin{definition}
   307	  \label{def:canonical-complement}
   308	  Let $E$ be the standard basis of linear space $V = \F^n$.
   309	  Let $F = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly
   310	  independent vectors in $V$.
   311	  The \emph{canonical complement $F^\perp$ of $F$} is the set of $n-m$ independent
   312	  vectors defined as follows.
   313	  Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i, j}\, \hat{e}_j$.
   314		Using a canonical algorithm for Gaussian elimination that works over arbitrary
   315	  fields, transform the $m\times n$ matrix $(a_{i, j})$ to reduced row echelon
   316	  form $(b_{i, j})$.
   317	  Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices of the leading $1$ entry in each row
   318	  of $(b_{i, j})$.
   319	  The canonical complement is defined as $F^\perp = \{ \hat{e}_j : j \not\in J \}$.
   320	\end{definition}
   321	
   322	
   323	\begin{remark}
   324	We emphasize that the canonical complement $F^\perp$ is a \emph{set} (rather than
   325	a subspace), and it is defined with respect to a \emph{set} of linearly
   326	independent vectors $F$. While there are equivalent ways of defining
   327	a canonical complement of a \emph{subspace} in a basis-independent manner, 
   328	we use this particular definition because it makes it clear that
   329	the canonical complement of a set $F$ is efficiently computable. 
   330	\end{remark}
   331	
   332	\begin{remark}
   333	  Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V$.
   334	  Suppose subspace $S$ is a register subspace of $V$ spanned by
   335	  $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$.
   336	  Then it is not hard to verify that the canonical complement of $\hat{E}_{0}$ is
   337	  $\hat{E}\setminus \hat{E}_0$ and the span of the canonical complement coincides with
   338	  $S^\perp$.
   339	\end{remark}
   340	
   341	
   342	\begin{lemma}
   343	  \label{lem:canonical-complement}
   344	  Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors $F = \{v_1,\ldots,v_m \}
   345	  \subseteq V$ and let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$ as defined
   346	  in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   347	  Let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   348	  Then
   349	  \begin{equation*}
   350	   \qquad S + T = V\;,  S \cap T = \{ 0 \} \;.
   351	  \end{equation*}
   352	\end{lemma}
   353	
   354	\begin{proof}
   355	To show the first item, we must show that every vector in $V$ can be
   356	written as a sum of an element of $S$ and an element of $T$. To do
   357	this, let $A = (a_{i, j})$ be the $m\times n$ matrix over $\F$ whose
   358	rows are the vectors $v_i$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   359	  Write $A = U B$ where $U$ is invertible and $B$ is in reduced row echelon
   360	  form.
   361	  Let $J$ be the set of column indices of the leading 1 entries in
   362	  $B$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.  
   363	  Now, the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span the subpsace $S$, and the restriction of
   364	  these rows to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   365	  span $\F^m$. Thus, for any vector $u \in V$, there is some linear
   366	  combination $v$ of rows of $B$ such that $u$ and $v$ agree
   367	  restricted to the columns in $J$. In other words, there exists $v
   368	  \in S$ such that $u_j = v_j$ for all $j \in J$. Hence, $u = v + w$
   369	  for $w \in T$, where $T$ is the canonical complement.
   370	  This shows $S + T = V$.
   371	  Counting dimensions shows that necessarily $S\cap T =
   372	  \{0\}$.
   373	\end{proof}
   374	
   375	\begin{definition}
   376	  \label{def:cl-canonical}
   377	  Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors.
   378	  Let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$.
   379	  Define the \emph{canonical linear map $L \in \End(V)$ with kernel basis $F$}
   380	  as the projector onto $T$ parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and $T
   381	  = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   382	  When the basis $F$ for $S$ is clear from context, we refer to this map as the
   383	  \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$.}
   384	\end{definition}
   385	
   386	\begin{definition}
   387	  \label{def:Lperp}
   388	  Let $L \in \End(V)$ be a linear map, and let $F$ be a basis for
   389	  $\ker(L)^\perp$.
   390	  Define $L^\perp : V \rightarrow V$ as the canonical linear map with kernel
   391	  basis $F$.
   392	\end{definition}
   393	
   394	\begin{lemma}
   395	  \label{lem:L_perp_perp}
   396	  Let $L \in \End(V)$ be a linear map and $F$ a basis for $\ker(L)^\perp$.
   397	  Let $L^\perp \in \End(V)$ be the linear map defined in
   398	  Definition~\ref{def:Lperp}.
   399	  Then $\ker(L^\perp) = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   400	\end{lemma}
   401	
   402	\begin{proof}
   403	  First, to set notation, let $S = \mathrm{span}(F) = \ker(L)^\perp$ and $T =
   404	  \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement},
   405	  any vector $v \in V$ can be uniquely decomposed as $v = v^S +
   406	  v^T$. 
   407	
   408	  Now we will show the lemma.  First we show that if $\ker(L^\perp) \subseteq \ker(L)^\perp$. Let
   409	  $v \in \ker(L^\perp)$, and write $v = v^S + v^T$.  By the definition
   410	  of $L^\perp$, it follows that $v^T = 0$, and hence $v \in S = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   420	\subsection{Finite fields}
   421	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   422	
   423	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ be a prime power.
   424	We denote the finite fields of $p$ and $q$ elements by $\Fp$ and $\Fq$
   425	respectively.
   426	The prime $p$ is the characteristic of field $\Fq$, and field $\Fp$ is the
   427	\emph{prime subfield} of $\Fq$.
   428	We sometimes omit the subscript and simply use $\F$ to denote the finite field
   429	when the size of the field is implicit from context.
   430	For general background on finite fields, and explicit algorithms for elementary
   431	arithmetic operations, we refer to~\cite{mullen2013handbook}.
   432	
   433	\subsubsection{Subfields and bases}
   434	\label{sec:subfields}
   435	Let $q$ be a prime power and $k$ an integer. 
   436	The field $\Fq$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of
   437	dimension $k$ over $\Fq$.
   438	Let $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ be a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ as a linear space over $\Fq$.
   439	Introduce a bijection $\downsize_q : \F_{q^k} \rightarrow \Fq^k$ between
   440	$\F_{q^k}$ and $\Fq^k$ defined with respect to the basis $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ by
   441	\begin{equation*}
   442	  \downsize_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k
   443	\end{equation*}
   444	where $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$.
   445	This map satisfies several nice properties.
   446	First, the map is an isomorphism of $\Fq$-vector spaces: it is $\Fq$-linear and addition in $\F_{q^k}$
   447	naturally corresponds to vector addition in $\Fq^k$.
   448	Namely, for all $a,b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   449	\begin{equation*}
   450		\downsize_q (a + b) = \downsize_q(a) + \downsize_q(b)\;.
   451	\end{equation*}
   452	Second, multiplication by a field element in $\F_{q^k}$ corresponds to a linear
   453	map on $\F_{q}^k$.
   454	For all $a \in \F_{q^k}$, there exists a matrix $K_a \in \Matrix_k (\Fq)$ such
   455	that for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   456	\begin{equation*}
   457		\downsize_q (a b) = K_a \, \downsize_q(b)\;.
   458	\end{equation*}
   459	The matrix $K_a$ is called the \emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to
   460	  basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$}.
   461	
   462	We extend the map $\downsize_q$ to vectors, matrices and sets over $\F_{q^k}$.
   463	For $v = (v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$, define
   464	\begin{equation*}
   465	  \downsize_q (v) = \bigl( \downsize_q (v_i) \bigr)_{i=1}^n \in \Fq^{kn}\;.
   466	\end{equation*}
   467	Similarly, for matrix $M = (M_{i, j}) \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$, define
   468	\begin{equation*}
   469	  \downsizem_q (M) = \bigl( K_{M_{i, j}} \bigr) \in \Matrix_{mk, nk} (\Fq)\;,
   470	\end{equation*}
   471	the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th block is the multiplication table $K_{M_{i,
   472	    j}}$ of $M_{i, j}$ with respect to basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$.
   473	For a set $S$ of vectors in $\F_{q^k}^n$, define
   474	\begin{equation*}
   475		\downsize_q(S) = \{ \downsize_q(v) : v \in S \}\;.
   476	\end{equation*}
   477	We omit the subscript and write $\downsize$ and $\downsizem$ for $\downsize_q$
   478	and $\downsizem_q$ respectively when $q$ equals to $p$, the characteristic of
   479	the field.
   480	
   481	The \emph{trace of\/ $\F_{q^k}$ over\/ $\Fq$} is defined as
   482	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   483	  \tr_{q^k \to q} :\; a \,\mapsto \, \Tr(K_a)
   484	\end{equation}
   485	for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $\Tr(K_a)$ is the trace of the multiplication table
   486	of $a$ with respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$.
   487	By definition, the trace is an $\Fq$-linear map from $\F_{q^k}$ to
   488	$\Fq$. The trace is in fact independent of the choice of basis, which
   489	can be seen from the following equivalent definition~\cite[Definition 2.1.80]{mullen2013handbook}:
   490	\[
   491		\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   492	\]
   493	
   494	A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', e_2', \ldots, e_k' \}$ of $\{e_1, e_2, \ldots,
   495	e_k\}$ is a basis such that $\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for
   496	all $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.
   497	A \emph{self-dual basis} is one that is equal to its dual.
   498	If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set $\{ \alpha^{q^j} \}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a
   499	basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\Fq$, the basis is called a \emph{normal
   500	  basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not exist for all fields but are guaranteed to exist under
   501	certain conditions; in particular, if $q = 2$ and $k$ is odd, as will
   502	be shown in \Cref{lem:efficient_basis}.
   503	
   504	We record some convenient facts about the maps $\downsize(\cdot)$ and
   505	$\downsizem(\cdot)$ for self-dual bases.
   506	
   507	\begin{lemma}
   508	  \label{lem:downsize_field}
   509	  Let $q$ be a prime power, $k$ an integer and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual basis for
   510	  $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   511	  The map $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ corresponding to $\{e_i\}$ satisfies the
   512	  following properties:
   513	  \begin{enumerate}
   514	  \item For all $x \in \F_{q^k}$, $\downsize_q(x) = \bigl( \tr_{q^k \to
   515	      q}(xe_1),\ldots,\tr_{q^k \to q}(xe_k) \bigr)$.
   516	  \item For all $x,y \in \F_{q^k}$, $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \downsize_q(x) \cdot
   517	    \downsize_q(y)$.
   518	  \item For all $M \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in
   519	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsizem_q(M) \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(Mv)$.
   520	  \end{enumerate}

   631	
   632	  There is a unique choice of coefficients $\alpha_{i, j} \in \F_q$ such that
   633	  $\downsize_q(z) = \sum_{i, j} \alpha_{i, j} \downsize_q(e_j v_i)$.
   634	  But then
   635	  \begin{align*}
   636	    \downsize_q(z) & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \bigl ( \sum_j
   637	                     \alpha_{i, j} e_j \bigr) v_i \Bigr) \\
   638	                   & = \downsize_q \Bigl( \sum_i \alpha_i v_i \Bigr)\;,
   639	  \end{align*}
   640	  where we define $\alpha_i = \sum_j \alpha_{i, j} e_j$.
   641	  Since $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is a bijection, this implies that $z = \sum_i
   642	  \alpha_i v_i$, and therefore $z^V = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i v_i$ (and similarly
   643	  $z^W = \sum_{i=m+1}^n \alpha_i v_i$).
   644	  This implies that
   645	  \begin{equation*}
   646		  \downsize_q(z)^{V'} = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j} \alpha_{i, j}
   647	    \downsize_q(e_j v_i) = \downsize_q (z^V)\;,
   648	  \end{equation*}
   649	  and similarly $\downsize_q(z)^{W'} = \downsize_q(z^W)$.
   650	  This completes the proof of the lemma.
   651	\end{proof}

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,
   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.
   810	  multiplication table $K_a$.
   811	
   812	  For the ``Furthermore'' part, we observe that since $\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m
   813	  \} \cup \{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_{n-m} \}$ forms a basis for $\F_{2^k}^n$, there
   814	  is a unique way to write $x$ as a $\F_{2^k}$ linear combination of $\{ v_i\}$
   815	  and $\{w_j\}$.
   816	  Via Gaussian elimination over $\F_{2^k}$, the $\F_2$-representation of the
   817	  coefficients of this linear combination can be computed in $\poly(n,k)$ time.
   818	  Here we use that addition, multiplication and division over $\F_{2^k}$ can be

   820	\end{proof}

   822	\begin{remark}
   823	  \label{rmk:tm_fields}
   824	  Throughout this paper, whenever we refer to Turing machines that perform

   832	\subsection{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   833	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   834	
   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.
   849	For one, the classical and quantum low-degree tests of \Cref{sec:ldt} are
   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).
   855	
   856	We recall the Schwartz-Zippel lemma: 
   857	
   858	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz-Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]
   859	  \label{lem:schwartz-zippel}

   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).
   885	For any such $a$ define the multilinear polynomial $g_a: \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   886	called the \emph{low-degree encoding of $a$}, as follows:
   887	\begin{equation}
   888	\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   889		 g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)\;.
   890	\end{equation}
   891	Note that for any $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_a(y) = a_y$.
   892	Furthermore, the map $a\mapsto g_a$ is linear: for every $x \in \F_q^m$,
   893	\begin{equation}
   894	\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   895		g_a(x) = a \cdot \ind_m(x)\;,
   896	\end{equation}
   897	where $\ind_m(x)$ is the vector $(\ind_{m,y}(x))_{y \in \{0,1\}^m}\in\F_q^M$.
   898	
   899	\begin{lemma}
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}

   957	\subsection{Measurements and observables}
   958	
   959	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued
   960	measures (POVMs).
   961	A POVM consists of a set of positive semidefinite operators $\{ M_a \}_{a\in S}$
   962	indexed by outcomes $a\in S$ that satisfy the condition $\sum_a M_a = I$. If the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \leq I$ then we refer to $\{M_a\}$ as a \emph{sub-measurement}.
   963	We sometimes use the same letter $M$ to refer to the collection of operators
   964	defining the POVM.
   965	The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on state $\ket{\psi}$
   966	is given by
   967	\begin{equation*}
   968	  \Pr(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\;.
   969	\end{equation*}
   970	A POVM $M=\{M_a\}$ is said to be \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a
   971	projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$). This automatically implies that operators
   972	$M_a, M_b$ for distinct outcomes $a \neq b$ are orthogonal ($M_a M_b =
   973	M_b M_a = 0$). An \emph{observable} is a unitary matrix.
   974	A \emph{binary observable} is an observable $O$ such that $O^2 = \Id$, i.e.\ $O$
   975	has eigenvalues in $\{-1,1\}$.
   976	
   977	We follow the convention that subscripts of the measurement index
   978	the outcome and superscripts of the measurement are used to index different
   979	measurements.
   980	For example, we use $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$ to represent a measurement indexed by $x$
   981	whose outcome consists of two parts $a$ and $b$.
   982	In this case, by slightly abusing the notation, we use $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$
   983	to denote
   984	\begin{equation*}
   985	  M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\, b}\;, \quad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\, b}\;.
   986	\end{equation*}
   987	For any $x$, $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$ are POVMs sometimes referred to as the
   988	``marginals'' of $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$.

  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform

  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.

# Proof Frontier Review

This document gives a checklist for reviewing Lean changes that introduce or
thread structure fields in the formalization. Its purpose is to prevent a
well-typed bookkeeping layer from being mistaken for a mathematical construction
theorem.

The central distinction is this:

- An **obligation discharger** derives a mathematical object or relation from
  the hypotheses appearing in the paper or blueprint.
- An **external residual** records a missing obligation discharger explicitly,
  with a named issue and a statement of the mathematical obstruction.
- A **bookkeeping conversion** changes the form or namespace of an already
  available object without deriving a new mathematical fact.

All three forms can be legitimate. The review problem is to identify which one
has been added, and to make sure the prose, blueprint tags, and issue status say
the same thing.

## Why Source-Level Holes Are Not Enough

The number of occurrences of `sorry` in the source is only a kernel-level
metric. It does not determine the mathematical frontier. A proof can be
`sorry`-free while still assuming the object that the paper asks one to
construct, for example by adding a field to a structure and proving the next
theorem by projecting that field.

For the LDT development this distinction matters most near the main theorem,
the main induction step, self-improvement, orthonormalization, and
projectivization. In these regions, a single displayed statement in the paper
usually depends on several intermediate constructions. Closing one local source
hole may only move the remaining obligation into an input structure.

## Reviewer Checklist

Before approving a PR that adds or modifies a structure field in a type named
with a suffix such as `Input`, `Residual`, `BridgeInputs`, `Witness`,
`Statement`, `Conclusion`, or `Obligations`, check the following points.

1. **Classify each new field.** State whether the field is produced in the PR,
   remains an external residual, or is only a bookkeeping conversion.
2. **Name the obligation discharger.** If the field is produced, cite the exact
   Lean theorem that derives it from the paper hypotheses. If no such theorem
   exists, keep the parent mathematical issue open and link a native sub-issue
   for the missing obligation.
3. **Check the blueprint frontier.** For work near `mainFormal`, Section 6,
   self-improvement, orthonormalization, or projectivization, inspect
   `blueprint/dep_graph_document.html` after building the blueprint. The
   remaining open vertices are part of the review context, even when the source
   diff contains no `sorry`.
4. **Reject hidden residual drift.** A theorem that merely moves an assumption
   into a structure field should be described as a conditional helper or a
   remaining obligation, not as proving the paper step.
5. **Review public prose.** Docstrings, module text, PR descriptions, and
   blueprint paragraphs should distinguish obligations proved from the paper
   hypotheses from inputs of conditional helpers and bookkeeping conversions.
6. **Size follow-up tasks by proof leaves.** Prefer issues such as "prove the
   raw Step 3 Cauchy--Schwarz estimate" to issues such as "close the
   self-improvement inputs" when the latter contains several independent
   proof obligations.
7. **Use native sub-issues.** Missing obligations should be linked under the
   correct parent tracker instead of being left only in a PR comment.

## Diagonal and Completion Data

The recent Section 6 and self-improvement work exposed several tracked
proof-obligation structures. They should be reviewed as debt to remove, not as
new source hypotheses to normalize. The recurring ambiguity is that a theorem
may mention diagonal data, completion data, or restricted strategy data while
only repackaging such data as an explicit input.

For any theorem whose name or docstring mentions diagonal consistency,
line-130 data, completion, restricted strategies, or repaired strategy data,
reviewers should ask the following mathematical question:

Does the theorem derive the stated object from the paper hypotheses, or does it
assume that object as a field?

For line 130 of `references/ldt-paper/inductive_step.tex`, in particular,
the paper supplies a cross relation between `G^A` and `G^B`. A Lean theorem
that consumes diagonal strong self-consistency of `G^A` or `G^B` should not be
described as deriving that diagonal input unless it contains the missing
argument.

## Blueprint Tags

Use `\leanok` only when the Lean declaration proves the mathematical assertion
of the blueprint node under the stated hypotheses. If the Lean declaration is a
conditional wrapper or input splitter, then the blueprint should say so
explicitly. It may still cite the declaration with `\lean{...}`, but the prose
must identify the remaining obligation.

When a PR introduces a public auxiliary lemma that is not a named paper
statement, the blueprint should either omit it or cite it as a subordinate
formalization-only support lemma. Do not allow a support lemma to inherit the
status of the paper theorem whose proof will eventually consume it.

## Examples From the Project

- Issue #1110 and the surrounding Section 6 work showed that diagonal and
  line-130 inputs can be made type-correct without proving the diagonal
  obligation. Such declarations must be described as conditional inputs.
- Issue #1109 concerned final-field boundedness. The generalized theorem
  `final_fields_bounded` is a genuine obligation discharger once the SDP dual
  witness satisfies `I <= Z`; the blueprint prose was updated to state that
  hypothesis and the theorem's actual generality.
- Issues #1070 and #1072 are examples of proof-frontier work where individual
  structure fields had to be separated from the mathematical obligation still
  tracked by the parent self-improvement issue.
- Issue #1081 and parent issue #931 illustrate why a parent tracker should stay
  open when a PR only supplies a conditional helper or residual record.

These examples are not special exceptions. They are the model for future review:
identify the mathematical obligation, name the residual when it remains, and
keep the public prose faithful to that distinction.

# Mathematical Language Guidelines

MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
the formalization with the paper and blueprint.

This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.

## Scope

These guidelines apply to:

- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
- module docstrings;
- declaration docstrings;
- documentation-visible section comments;
- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
- issue titles and issue bodies;
- PR titles and PR descriptions.

## Source of Truth

Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:

1. `references/ldt-paper/`
2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files

When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.

## Reference Notation And Terminology

The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.

When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
first applicable location in the following order:

1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
   differs from the paper;
2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
   family of declarations in that file;
3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
   blueprint;
4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.

The explanation should say:

- the notation or term used in the paper;
- the Lean object or name which represents it;
- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
- the scope in which the replacement should be used.

A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
where future readers can learn it.

Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.

## Naming Norm

Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled.

Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
clearer phrase.

This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
number, or implementation history.

### Concrete examples

The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
paper or blueprint would recognize.

| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |

An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.

File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.

### Shared helpers

When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.

Procedure:

1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   explicit argument.
2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   blueprint location it supports.

### Legacy identifier treatment

If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.

Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.

## Review Checklist

Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.

- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
      implementation-phase labels)?
- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
      source does not use them that way?
- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
      that order of preference?
- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
      construction they support?
- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.

Review-fix PRs touching a surface covered by an active audit should read the
relevant audit before changing names or prose.

# Lean Proof-Evasion Anti-Patterns

Catalog of subtle proof-evasion patterns that pass kernel-level checks
(`sorry`-free, no forbidden tactics, all axioms standard) yet still fail to
prove the claimed mathematics. Complements
the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference, which covers the kernel-level
blockers; this file covers patterns where the Lean code *compiles and the
trick is at the level of what the statement says or what the definitions
bake in*.

Every pattern here is **castle-in-the-air in spirit**: a theorem named after a
paper result that doesn't actually prove it. The named offenders below all
cross-reference a concrete issue or PR so reviewers can see a real example.

## Why this matters

Kernel checks are necessary but not sufficient. A theorem can:

- Be marked `\leanok` in the blueprint,
- Have a sorry-free proof body,
- Have a clean axiom closure (`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` only),

and still prove **nothing that the paper actually claims**, if the proof
obligation has been displaced into a hypothesis, a definition, or a sentinel
branch. The patterns below are the displacement mechanisms we've seen in this
codebase.

## Catalogue

- [A1 — Conclusion-shaped hypothesis](#a1--conclusion-shaped-hypothesis)
- [A2 — Definitional sleight-of-hand](#a2--definitional-sleight-of-hand)
- [A3 — Zero-fallback branches hiding preconditions](#a3--zero-fallback-branches-hiding-preconditions)
- [A4 — Trivial default witnesses for existentials](#a4--trivial-default-witnesses-for-existentials)
- [A5 — Castle-in-the-air / bypassing Mathlib](#a5--castle-in-the-air--bypassing-mathlib)
- [A6 — External `*Statement` smuggles](#a6--external-statement-smuggles)

---

## A1 — Conclusion-shaped hypothesis

**Smell.** The theorem takes a hypothesis whose type is the theorem's own
conclusion (or an `∃`/function that produces the conclusion). The proof body
is a trivial `rcases`/`exact`/`.trans`/`simpa using h` and does no
mathematical work. A variant wraps the hypothesis in a named bundle
(`*BridgePackage`, `*Statement`); see issues [#449], [#451], [#477] for the
catalogue, and [#493] for the inline-existential mutation triggered by
PR [#491].

### Why it's bad

The theorem's named mathematical content is never derived from prior lemmas;
the caller (who supplies the hypothesis) has to discharge it. In practice the
caller then has the same problem, pushing the obligation further up the
stack. The theorem is true under a vacuous hypothesis and the `\leanok` tag
misrepresents the actual state of the proof.

### How to spot it

- The hypothesis type contains, up to `∃` / `∧` / a coercion, the theorem's
  conclusion.
- The proof body is one of:
  - `rcases h with ⟨...⟩; exact ⟨...⟩`
  - `exact h.fieldName` / `exact h.a.trans h.b`
  - `by simpa using h.fieldName`
- The hypothesis is a bundle named `*BridgePackage`, `*Witness`, `*Package`,
  `*Output`, with a field whose type matches the conclusion structure.
- Consumers of the bundle are trivial (field projection + return).

### Concrete example

Historical example (before the MainInductionStep cleanup):

```lean
theorem mainInduction
    (params : Parameters) [FieldModel params.q]
    (strategy : SymStrat params ι)
    (eps delta gamma : Error) (k : ℕ)
    (hbridge : MainInductionBridgePackage params strategy eps delta gamma k) :
    ∃ G : Measurement (Polynomial params) ι,
      ConsRel strategy.state ...
        (mainInductionError params k eps delta gamma) := by
  rcases hbridge.witness with ⟨error, G, hG, herror⟩
  refine ⟨G, ?_⟩
  exact ⟨le_trans hG.offDiagonalBound herror⟩
```

Here `MainInductionBridgePackage.witness` has type
`∃ error, ∃ G, ConsRel ... error ∧ error ≤ mainInductionError ...` — literally
the conclusion. The code has since been refactored to remove both this
specific MainInductionStep bridge and the interim theorem alias that exposed
the same witness shape under the paper theorem's name, but the snippet remains
the archetypal example of the anti-pattern.

PR [#491] proposed to delete the `*BridgePackage` by **inlining** the bundle's
fields as explicit hypotheses. That only scatters the same pattern across
individual signatures without producing any proof — it's strictly worse
because the named bundle at least shows up in one tracker. Do not accept PRs
that discharge an ungrounded bridge by flattening it into conclusion-shaped
existential hypotheses, or by reintroducing the same shape under a theorem name
that suggests the paper result has been proved.

### How to fix it

Prefer **proving a real intermediate lemma** — one that the paper also uses
— and stating its signature with the paper's hypotheses (not the theorem's
conclusion). Then use it inside the larger theorem. If the missing content
cannot be formalized yet, state the missing assertion as a named obligation
to be proved from the paper hypotheses, and leave the corresponding proof open
under a tracker. Do not put that obligation on the source-labelled theorem as
an extra hypothesis. Existing `BridgePackage`-style declarations are proof
debt to be removed or converted into source-faithful obligations; they are not
the preferred shape for new work.

A signature passes the smell test if:

- Every hypothesis is a **named intermediate fact** that also appears in the
  paper or blueprint proof, not the theorem's output packaged up, and
- Replacing a hypothesis with its negation would produce a *different*
  theorem, not a trivially-false one.

## A2 — Definitional sleight-of-hand

**Smell.** A `def`/`abbrev` is written so its body is the paper's claim, and
a nearby `theorem` restates that claim and proves it by `rfl` (or a one-line
`simp [foo]` where `foo` is the defining equation). The "mathematical
content" has been baked into the definition; the theorem is a tautology. See
issues [#477], [#494].

### Why it's bad

`rfl` proves that a definition equals itself. If the definition is chosen
*so that* it equals the conclusion, the `rfl` "proof" transports none of the
paper's reasoning — it is literally the reflexivity of a shape we invented to
match the conclusion. The real identity the paper proves (e.g.,
`⟨φ_α, φ_β⟩ = δ_αβ` over an actual inner product) is still not stated
anywhere in Lean.

### How to spot it

- A `theorem` whose body is `rfl` / `by rfl` / `by simp [defName]` where
  `defName` is the def that unfolds to the conclusion.
- A `structure` with a `Prop`-typed field whose *role* in the paper is a
  nontrivial identity (SVD, orthonormality, Cauchy–Schwarz), accompanied by a
  constructor that discharges that field with `rfl`.
- A `def foo := if α = β then 1 else 0` followed by a theorem asserting
  `foo α β = if α = β then 1 else 0`.
- Bridge-like structures where every field is itself a function
  `(precondition) → (conclusion-step)` and the consumer applies the field
  directly.

### Concrete example

From `MIPStarRE/LDT/ExpansionHypercubeGraph/Defs/Fourier.lean`:

```lean
/-- The exact inner-product formula for the hypercube Fourier basis. -/
def fourierBasisInnerProduct (params : Parameters)
    (α β : Point params) : Error :=
  if α = β then 1 else 0

/-- The exact inner-product formula for the hypercube Fourier basis. -/
lemma fourierBasisInnerProduct_eq (params : Parameters)
    (α β : Point params) :
    fourierBasisInnerProduct params α β = if α = β then 1 else 0 := rfl

/-- `prop:eigenvectors`. -/
theorem eigenvectors (params : Parameters) :
    (∀ α β : Point params,
      fourierBasisInnerProduct params α β = if α = β then 1 else 0) ∧ ... := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · intro α β
    exact fourierBasisInnerProduct_eq params α β    -- castle: def IS Kronecker delta
  ...
```

The paper's orthonormality claim — that the additive characters `φ_α` form an
orthonormal basis under the actual inner product
`⟨f, g⟩ := (1/|V|) · ∑_u f(u)^* · g(u)` — requires a genuine character-sum
identity. The Lean theorem states and proves only the trivial fact that the
definition equals itself.

### Not every `rfl` is a castle

Distinguish from legitimate bookkeeping where a named equation is literally
how something was defined. Example: `mainFormalError_eq_envelope` in
`Test/ErrorCascade/Definitions.lean` unfolds the definition of
`mainFormalError` to its envelope factorization. The mathematical content is
elsewhere (the envelope is derived from per-step bounds); the `rfl` theorem is
a naming convenience only. The test is: **does the `def` body encode a paper
identity, or does it just name a compound expression?**

### How to fix it

1. Move the paper's real definition to the concrete one: for Fourier, define
   the inner product as the actual sum over vertices, and the characters
   `φ_α` as functions from `Point params` to `ℂ`.
2. State the paper's identity (`⟨φ_α, φ_β⟩ = δ_αβ`) as a theorem over those
   concrete objects.
3. Prove it via the standard character-sum derivation (or cite the Mathlib
   counterpart if one exists — `Matrix.dotProduct` / `Finset.sum_eq_zero_iff`
   combined with `ZMod.sum_pow_units` style lemmas).
4. If you want to keep the Kronecker shorthand, define it *afterward* as a
   consequence, not as the primitive.

## A3 — Zero-fallback branches hiding preconditions

**Smell.** A total function is defined by `if eligible then real_value else
default`, where the `default` (usually `0`, `default`, `⊥`, or
`Classical.arbitrary`) is a sentinel for "precondition not met." Downstream
theorems state properties that are only true on the eligible branch, but the
theorem's type signature does not carry the eligibility proof, so the
obligation moves silently from the prover to whoever happens to call the
function. See issue [#495], related to [#307].

### Why it's bad

The signature lies about the domain of validity. A caller passing a
non-eligible input gets `0` back; any theorem proved about "the output" is
proved for `0`, which is trivially true and carries no information. When a
later theorem composes the output with another lemma, the composition
type-checks but the conclusion is vacuous on inputs where the original
precondition failed.

The paper, by contrast, restricts the quantifier in the first place:
"Fix a tuple `(x₁, ..., x_k)` with Hamming weight `≥ d+1`." The Lean should
match.

### How to spot it

- `match ... with | some _ => real | none => 0` or `| _ => 0`.
- `if hEligible : P then ... else default`.
- Identifier names containing `fallback`, `placeholder`, `sentinel`,
  `dummy`, `or0`, `orDefault`.
- Recursive definitions whose base case unconditionally returns a sentinel.
- Functions that return `Polynomial params` but can return the zero polynomial
  on inputs that shouldn't be in the domain.

### Concrete example (historical; resolved by PR #561)

Until PR #561, `MIPStarRE/LDT/Pasting/Defs/Interpolation.lean` contained:

```lean
/-- Extract the polynomial from a completed slice outcome; returns 0 on ⊥. -/
noncomputable def extractSliceOr0 {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]
    (g : GHatOutcome params) : PolynomialModel params :=
  match g with
  | some p => p.poly
  | none   => 0
```

The consumer `interpolateCompletedSlicesFromSupport` ran Lagrange
interpolation on `extractSliceOr0`-extracted values. If the support contained
a `none`, the interpolant silently pretended that slice evaluated to zero.
The paper's Lagrange step is quantified over *eligible* slices only, so the
Lean API should carry `∀ i ∈ support, (g i).isSome` as a hypothesis; instead
it carried nothing, and the theorem technically type-checked on inputs for
which its conclusion was meaningless.

**Current status:** resolved. The live API now removes `extractSliceOr0`,
threads the explicit hypothesis `hσsupport : σ ⊆ gHatTupleSupport gs` into
`interpolateCompletedSlicesFromSupport`, and packages the chosen support subset
as `InterpolationSupportWitness` so the arbitrary choice and its proof fields
are visible at call sites.

### Acceptable uses of this pattern

Not every default branch is a castle. `Inhabited` / `Nonempty` instances
that provide a canonical inhabitant (e.g., the zero polynomial for
`Nonempty (Polynomial params)`) are plumbing, not proof. The test is: **does
any theorem mention the output?** If a theorem says "the output satisfies
P", and P is not trivially satisfied by the sentinel, the fallback is
smuggling a precondition.

### How to fix it

Pick one of:

1. **Make the precondition explicit.** Add `(h : eligible input) :` to the
   signature. Let Lean's type system enforce that non-eligible inputs cannot
   be passed.
2. **Return an `Option`.** The `none` result forces every caller to handle
   the case, so theorems about "the output" now quantify only over the
   `some` branch.
3. **Restrict the domain.** Instead of `(x : X) → Y`, take `(x : {x : X //
   P x}) → Y`. Common for finite-support Lagrange-style constructions where
   the subtype is computable via `Finset.filter`.

### Classical-logic dependencies

A sibling smell in this pattern: `DecidablePred` / `DecidableEq` instances
that silently use `Classical.dec` to fill in decidability that should be
constructive. The historical `interpolationEligibleSandwichFamily`
implementation was exactly such a case: it used `open Classical in ...` to
gate a predicate that is actually decidable by a finite-support check. PR
#561 fixed that example by adding `interpolationEligible_decidablePred`.
Those classical instances are acceptable only when the predicate is genuinely
non-constructive; if a constructive instance is plausible, write it, don't
bottom out in `Classical.dec`. See [#495] for the full catalogue of
classical-logic uses in `LDT/Pasting/`.

**Smell.** A theorem of the shape `∃ x, P x` is closed by picking

   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}

    30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.

   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

   178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.
   238	
   239	
   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}
